For $I,J$ small filtered, $K:I\to C$ and $T:J\to C$, put \[ h_K(X)=\colim_{i\in I}\Hom_C(X,K_i),\qquad \Hom_{\Ind C}(K,T)=\lim_{i\in I}\colim_{j\in J}\Hom_C(K_i,T_j). \] The association $K\mapsto h_K$ is fully faithful. Under the hypotheses of A.3, $\Ind L\dashv\Ind R$ and $\Ind R$ is fully faithful. For an ind-object $K$, the following are equivalent: $h_K$ inverts $W_L$; it inverts all $\eta_X$ for $X\in C$; the unit $K\to(\Ind R)(\Ind L)K$ is invertible; $K$ belongs to the essential image of $\Ind R$; and the canonical comparison \[ h_K(X)\longrightarrow \Hom_{\Ind D}(LX,(\Ind L)K) \] is bijective for every $X\in C$. These are precisely the valid, typed contents of V ms.~40--42.
where_proved: sections/A.tex, statement A.4 and following proof/discussion; PDF p. 4

statement: The precise model-category mapping formula: Thomason's model category has weak equivalences $\W_\infty$ and fibrations detected by $\operatorname{Ex}^2N$. Its adjunction \[ c\operatorname{Sd}^2:\mathbf{sSet}\rightleftarrows\Cat: \operatorname{Ex}^2N \] is a Quillen equivalence. Choose a fibrant replacement $K\to RK$ in this model category. Put $QX=c\operatorname{Sd}^2NX$. The composite last-vertex map gives a natural weak equivalence $q_X:QX\to X$, and $QX$ is cofibrant. There are natural bijections \[ [BX,BK]\cong\pi_0\Map_{\mathbf{sSet}}(NX,\operatorname{Ex}^2NRK) \cong\Fun(QX,RK)_0/\sim_T . \] Here $\Fun(QX,RK)_0$ is the set of functors, and $\sim_T$ is generated by endpoint restrictions of functors $c\operatorname{Sd}^2(NX\times\Delta^1)\to RK$. For any cofibrant replacement $Q'X\to X$, one may equivalently use $\Hom_{\Cat}(Q'X,RK)$ modulo model-category homotopy. The displayed explicit relation specifies that homotopy; it does not silently replace it by a different cylinder relation.
where_proved: sections/A.tex, statement A.5 and following proof/discussion; PDF p. 5
notes: Exact model-cylinder relation; the source is replaced and the target is fibrant.

statement: A fibrant target does not suffice: The assertion that $\pi_0\Fun(X,P)\to[BX,BP]$ is always a bijection for a Thomason-fibrant $P$ is false, even for a finite $X$. The assertion that $\Fun(X,P)$ is always Thomason-fibrant is also false, even for a finite $X$ and a countable fibrant $P$.
where_proved: sections/A.tex, statement A.6 and following proof/discussion; PDF p. 5
notes: Two distinct counterexamples; finite ingredient checks in a_finite_checks.py.

statement: Descent of ind-representability needs no right adjoint: Let $L:C\to D$ be any localization, and let $H=\colim_{i\in I}h_{K_i}$ be a small filtered colimit of representable presheaves. If $H\cong H' L^{\op}$, then the canonical comparison identifies \[ H'\cong\colim_{i\in I}\Hom_D(-,LK_i). \] For a single representing object, it follows that $h_K$ inverts the localized class if and only if its canonical comparison with $\Hom_D(L-,LK)$ is bijective. This assertion, and not a reflection, is sufficient for the descent of the manuscript's external Hom ind-objects.
where_proved: sections/A.tex, statement A.7 and following proof/discussion; PDF p. 6

statement: What a sufficiently large group sees in a small category: Let $K$ be a $\U$-small category and let $G$ be a $\U$-small group such that every group homomorphism $G\longrightarrow H$ is trivial whenever $|H|\leq |\Mor K|$. The constant-functor map and evaluation map \[ \delta_K:K\longrightarrow\Fun(\mathsf B G,K),\qquad \operatorname{ev}_*: \Fun(\mathsf B G,K)\longrightarrow K \] are mutually inverse isomorphisms of categories. Consequently the map \[ p^*:\Hom_{\Cathot}(e,K)\longrightarrow \Hom_{\Cathot}(\mathsf B G,K),\qquad p:\mathsf B G\longrightarrow e, \] is a bijection. Both assertions are natural in $K$ among categories whose automorphism groups receive only trivial homomorphisms from $G$.
where_proved: sections/BC.tex, statement B.1 and following proof/discussion; PDF p. 7
notes: Includes empty categories and noninvertible endomorphisms.

statement: The finite Schur-multiplier input: For a finite set $F$ with $|F|\geq8$, \[ H_1(\operatorname{Alt}(F);\Z)=0, \qquad H_2(\operatorname{Alt}(F);\Z)\cong\Z/2. \] If $a,b,c,d$ are distinct elements of $F$, the commuting permutations $x=(ab)(cd)$ and $y=(ac)(bd)$ define a torus class \[ t_F=[x\mid y]-[y\mid x]\in H_2(\operatorname{Alt}(F);\Z) \] which generates this group. In particular, inclusions between finite alternating groups on sets containing these four elements and having at least eight elements carry generator to generator.
where_proved: sections/BC.tex, statement B.2 and following proof/discussion; PDF p. 7
notes: Finite upper bound is an imported classical theorem; transition maps checked using a fixed generator; exact Clifford algebra check attached.

statement: Finitary alternating groups at every infinite cardinal: Let $\Omega$ be an infinite $\U$-small set and let $A_\Omega=\operatorname{Alt}_{\mathrm{fin}}(\Omega)$ be the group of even permutations with finite support. Then \[ |A_\Omega|=|\Omega|,\qquad A_\Omega\text{ is nonabelian simple},\qquad H_1(A_\Omega;\Z)=0,\quad H_2(A_\Omega;\Z)=\Z/2. \] Every homomorphism from $A_\Omega$ to a group of cardinality strictly less than $|\Omega|$ is trivial.
where_proved: sections/BC.tex, statement B.3 and following proof/discussion; PDF p. 8
notes: Simplicity proved with fresh-point commutator; bar complexes give filtered homology colimit with verified transition maps.

statement: The asserted right adjoint and the first proposed envelope: There is no $\U$-small category $K$ representing \[ X\longmapsto [BX,K(\Z/2,2)] \quad\text{on }\Cathot^{\op}. \] Consequently $\varphi:\Cathot\to\Hot$ has no right adjoint, fully faithful or otherwise. The assertion at V~ms.~37 and the unrestricted Thomason--Kan-envelope construction at V~ms.~42--43 are false.
where_proved: sections/BC.tex, statement B.4 and following proof/discussion; PDF p. 8
his_places: V ms.37--43; III-V companion unproved reflection block
notes: Refutes existence of any right adjoint, not only a fully faithful one.

statement: A simple overgroup with a prescribed infinite cardinality: Let $H$ be a $\U$-small group and let $\lambda$ be an infinite $\U$-cardinal with $|H|\leq\lambda$. There is an injective homomorphism $H\hookrightarrow S$ into a nonabelian simple $\U$-small group $S$ with $|S|=\lambda$.
where_proved: sections/BC.tex, statement B.5 and following proof/discussion; PDF p. 9
notes: Explicit free-product word w=[g,t][g,t^2] and HNN relations put every h in normal closure of g; cardinal bound checked.

statement: An acyclic overgroup without a cardinal increase: For every infinite $\U$-small group $H$ there is an injective homomorphism $H\hookrightarrow M(H)$ with \[ |M(H)|=|H|,\qquad \widetilde H_i(BM(H);\Z)=0 \quad\text{for every }i\geq0. \] For a finite $H$, the same construction gives a countable overgroup.
where_proved: sections/BC.tex, statement B.6 and following proof/discussion; PDF p. 10
notes: Mitosis construction and field-homology annihilation proof supplied.

statement: Acyclic simple overgroups of arbitrary size: For every group $H$ and every infinite $\U$-cardinal $\lambda\geq\max(|H|,\aleph_0)$ there is a monomorphism of groups $i:H\hookrightarrow A$ such that $A$ is nonabelian simple, $|A|=\lambda$, and $BA$ is integrally acyclic.
where_proved: sections/BC.tex, statement B.7 and following proof/discussion; PDF p. 10
notes: Alternating injective simple and acyclic envelopes; no priority claimed.

statement: Groups invisible to smaller groups and mapping to spheres: For every integer $n\geq2$ and every infinite $\U$-cardinal $\lambda$ there is a $\U$-small group $G_{n,\lambda}$ and a pointed continuous map of CW models \[ q_{n,\lambda}:BG_{n,\lambda}\longrightarrow S^n \] such that $|G_{n,\lambda}|=\lambda$, the map $q_{n,\lambda}$ induces isomorphisms on integral homology in all degrees, and every homomorphism from $G_{n,\lambda}$ to a group of cardinality less than $\lambda$ is trivial. The group $G_{n,\lambda}$ is perfect. It is not asserted to be simple.
where_proved: sections/BC.tex, statement B.8 and following proof/discussion; PDF p. 11
notes: Iterated amalgamated doubles over acyclic simple envelopes; group need not itself be simple.

statement: The target condition needed to use these homology equivalences: Let $u:A\to B$ be a pointed integral homology equivalence between connected CW spaces, and let $Z$ be a pointed simply connected CW space. Precomposition induces a weak equivalence of derived pointed mapping spaces \[ u^*:\Map_*(B,Z)\longrightarrow\Map_*(A,Z). \] In particular it induces a bijection $[B,Z]_*\to[A,Z]_*$.
where_proved: sections/BC.tex, statement B.9 and following proof/discussion; PDF p. 12
notes: Full Postnikov mapping-space argument handles infinite towers and avoids phantom-map inference.

statement: Essential maps from arbitrarily large groups for every higher type: Let $Y$ be a $\U$-small homotopy type with a point $y$ and a nonzero element $\alpha\in\pi_n(Y,y)$ for some $n\geq2$. For every infinite $\U$-cardinal $\lambda$, the group $G_{n,\lambda}$ of B.8 has no nontrivial homomorphism to any group of cardinality less than $\lambda$ and admits a map $BG_{n,\lambda}\to Y$ which is not freely homotopic to a constant map. Thus this assertion holds for every homotopy type that is not a $1$-type, including every simply connected noncontractible homotopy type.
where_proved: sections/BC.tex, statement B.10 and following proof/discussion; PDF p. 12
notes: Universal-cover lifting proves non-nullness for arbitrary nontrivial pi_1 action.

statement: The full negative representability statement: For every $\U$-small homotopy type $Y$ which is not a $1$-type, the presheaf $X\mapsto[BX,Y]$ on $\Cathot$ is not representable by a $\U$-small category. No connectedness assumption on $Y$ is needed.
where_proved: sections/BC.tex, statement B.11 and following proof/discussion; PDF p. 13
notes: Naturality of constant-map square handles disconnected targets and infinite component sets.

statement: Groupoids are local, with the canonical comparison: For every $\U$-small category $X$ and $\U$-small groupoid $G$, the canonical map \[ \pi_0\Fun(X,G)\longrightarrow[BX,BG] \] is a bijection, natural in both variables. More precisely, \[ N\Fun(X,G)\cong\operatorname{Map}_{\mathrm{sSet}}(NX,NG) \] is an isomorphism of simplicial sets, and the right side is a derived mapping space. Restriction along $\eta_X$ is an isomorphism of categories $\Fun(\Pi_1X,G)\to\Fun(X,G)$.
where_proved: sections/BC.tex, statement C.1 and following proof/discussion; PDF p. 13
notes: NFun(X,G) is exactly the Kan derived simplicial mapping space.

statement: Classification of all representable homotopy types: A $\U$-small homotopy type $Y$ has its presheaf $X\mapsto[BX,Y]$ represented on $\Cathot$ by a $\U$-small category if and only if $Y$ is a $1$-type. If $Y$ is a $1$-type, a fundamental groupoid $G_Y$ represents it. Every other representing category is isomorphic to $G_Y$ in $\Cathot$, and its classifying space is isomorphic to $Y$ in $\Hot$. This is a complete affirmative answer to Lead~2's representability conjecture.
where_proved: sections/BC.tex, statement C.2 and following proof/discussion; PDF p. 14
notes: Includes empty and disconnected types; specified universal element is a weak equivalence in Hot.

statement: Classification of local categories: For a $\U$-small category $K$, the following conditions are equivalent: the canonical function $\pi_0\Fun(X,K)\to[BX,BK]$ is bijective for every $\U$-small $X$; the category $K$ is isomorphic in $\Cathot$ to a groupoid; and the canonical functor $\eta_K:K\to\Pi_1K$ is an isomorphism in $\Cathot$. In particular every local $K$ has $BK$ a $1$-type. Conversely, for a category with $BK$ a $1$-type, localness is equivalent to being isomorphic in $\Cathot$ to its groupoidification. The hypothesis that $BK$ is a $1$-type alone is insufficient.
where_proved: sections/BC.tex, statement C.3 and following proof/discussion; PDF p. 14
notes: Localness forces a 1-type; the converse from nerve 1-type alone fails.

statement: The reflector is fundamental groupoidification: Let $\mathcal L\subset\Cathot$ be the full subcategory of local objects. It is reflective. After identifying it with groupoids modulo natural isomorphism, its reflector is \[ \Pi_1:\Cathot\longrightarrow\operatorname{Ho}(\mathrm{Grpd}), \qquad \Pi_1\dashv I, \] where $I$ is the full inclusion and the unit is $[\eta_X]$. This reflector inverts exactly those functors that induce a bijection on components and isomorphisms on fundamental groups at every basepoint. Its unit is in $W_\infty$ precisely when $BX$ is a $1$-type. In particular this reflection does not supply the nonexistent right adjoint to $\varphi:\Cathot\to\Hot$.
where_proved: sections/BC.tex, statement C.4 and following proof/discussion; PDF p. 15
notes: This reflector inverts W_1, not merely W_infty; unit is W_infty exactly for 1-types.

statement: Coreflectivity, and the weaker converse from the classifying space: The inclusion $I:\mathcal L\hookrightarrow\Cathot$ has no right adjoint. Moreover, a category with contractible classifying space need not be local.
where_proved: sections/BC.tex, statement C.5 and following proof/discussion; PDF p. 15
notes: Infinite fence and discrete N source give a uniform-length obstruction; finite truncation checks attached.

statement: Thomason fibrancy is not the manuscript's localness: It is false that every Thomason-fibrant category is local in the sense of C.3. There is no change of target by a $W_\infty$-equivalence that makes a homotopy type with nonzero higher homotopy groups into a local category.
where_proved: sections/BC.tex, statement C.6 and following proof/discussion; PDF p. 16
notes: Fibrant replacement of a category of type S^2 has a higher type and is not local.

statement: Exact bounded representability: Let $Y$ be a $\U$-small Kan complex and let $\lambda\in\U$ be an infinite cardinal with $|Y|\leq\lambda$, where size counts simplices in all degrees. There is a $\U$-small category $K_\lambda(Y)$ and a natural transformation \[ \theta_{X,\lambda}:\pi_0\Fun(X,K_\lambda(Y))\longrightarrow[NX,Y] \qquad (X\in\Cat_\U) \] which is bijective whenever $|\Mor X|\leq\lambda$. One can take $|\Mor K_\lambda(Y)|\leq2^\lambda$. Consequently, for every infinite $\kappa\in\U$, the functor in Part D(i), on categories with fewer than $\kappa$ arrows, is represented by a small category after allowing the representing category to exceed the test bound.
where_proved: sections/D.tex, statement D.1 and following proof/discussion; PDF p. 16
notes: Explicit at-most-2^lambda arrow bound; natural comparison proved for all sources within lambda.

statement: Finite targets are not enough in the test examples: On the full category of finite categories, neither $X\mapsto[BX,S^2]$ nor $X\mapsto[BX,K(C_2,2)]$ has a finite representing category in $\Cathot$. Both have small, generally infinite, representing categories by D.1. For $K(C_2,2)$ and an uncountable limit cardinal $\kappa$, a representative for all tests with fewer than $\kappa$ arrows cannot itself have fewer than $\kappa$ arrows.
where_proved: sections/D.tex, statement D.2 and following proof/discussion; PDF p. 17

statement: Finite categories always give a filtered ind-representation: Let $\mathcal C_f$ be a skeleton of finite categories in $\Cathot$, with all functors modulo natural-transformation zigzags as morphisms. For every $\U$-small homotopy type $Y$, put $F_Y(C)=[BC,Y]$. The category of elements $\mathcal E_Y$ of $F_Y|_{\mathcal C_f}$ is a small filtered category, and \[ F_Y|_{\mathcal C_f}\cong \colim_{(C,c)\in\mathcal E_Y}\Hom_{\Cathot}(-,C)|_{\mathcal C_f}. \] Thus Part D(ii) has an affirmative answer for filtered ind-representability by finite categories. The assertion does not require that a finite category have homotopy-finite nerve.
where_proved: sections/D.tex, statement D.3 and following proof/discussion; PDF p. 18
notes: Index is arbitrary small filtered; no unsupported strictification of a general filtered Cathot diagram.

statement: The exact sequential criterion: For $Y\in\Hot_\U$, the restriction $F_Y|_{\mathcal C_f}$ is a colimit of a sequence of representables by finite categories if and only if $[BC,Y]$ is countable for every finite category $C$. Such a sequence may be represented by actual functors of finite categories. Its colimit $K$ in $\Cat$ is a countable locally finite category and represents $F_Y$ on finite tests. Conversely, every countable locally finite representing category supplies such a sequence. Here a category is locally finite when each finitely generated subcategory has finitely many arrows.
where_proved: sections/D.tex, statement D.4 and following proof/discussion; PDF p. 18
notes: Sequential strictification only; the colimit is locally finite without requiring injective transitions.

statement: The Eilenberg--Mac Lane sequential example: For $Y=K(C_2,2)$, the restriction to finite categories is ind-representable by a sequence of finite categories and representable by a countable locally finite category, although it is not representable on all $\Cathot_\U$ by any $\U$-small category.
where_proved: sections/D.tex, statement D.5 and following proof/discussion; PDF p. 19

statement: The sequential two-sphere test: The remaining exact question in Part D(ii) for $Y=S^2$ is whether $[BC,S^2]$ is countable for every finite category $C$. By D.4 this is equivalent to sequential ind-representability by finite categories; it is also equivalent to representability on finite tests by a countable locally finite category. General filtered ind-representability and ordinary small representability on these tests are already proved in D.3 and D.1. No assertion of sequential representability for $S^2$ is certified here.
where_proved: sections/D.tex, statement D.6 and following proof/discussion; PDF p. 19
notes: Open in this audit; not a claim of absence of a result in the literature.

statement: The unbounded cardinal-indexed representation: There is a compatible choice of the categories $K_\lambda(Y)$ for $\lambda\geq\max(\aleph_0,|Y|)$ and inclusion functors for increasing $\lambda$, such that, in the larger universe $\V$, \[ [B-,Y]\cong\colim_{\lambda\in\operatorname{Card}(\U),\ \lambda\geq\max(\aleph_0,|Y|)} \Hom_{\Cathot_\U}(-,K_\lambda(Y)). \] The indexing poset is filtered, $\V$-small, and unbounded in the $\U$-cardinals. Alternatively $F_Y$ is a $\V$-small filtered colimit over its category of elements on all $\Cathot_\U$.
where_proved: sections/D.tex, statement D.7 and following proof/discussion; PDF p. 19

statement: Why the larger index is necessary: If $Y$ has a component with a nonzero homotopy group in degree at least two, $F_Y$ on all $\Cathot_\U$ is not a $\U$-small colimit of representables, even without requiring the colimit to be filtered. If $Y$ is a 1-type it is representable by its fundamental groupoid. Thus, for the global functor, enlarging the index universe in D.7 is essential exactly outside the 1-types.
where_proved: sections/D.tex, statement D.8 and following proof/discussion; PDF p. 20
notes: Rules out any U-small indexing category, not merely filtered ones.

statement: The bounded conclusion also follows from Raptis's model structures: Let $\mu\in\U$ be a regular infinite cardinal. There is a model structure $\Cat_{I(\mu)}$ with weak equivalences $\W_\infty$ in which every $\mu$-presentable category is cofibrant. If $K\to R_\mu K$ is a fibrant replacement in this structure, then the canonical comparison \[ \pi_0\Fun(X,R_\mu K)\longrightarrow[BX,BK] \] is a bijection for every $\mu$-presentable $X$, in particular for every $X$ with fewer than $\mu$ arrows. Thus bounded representability is also a consequence of a known model structure; the construction in D.1 additionally gives its explicit size bound and compatible cardinal filtration.
where_proved: sections/D_model.tex, statement D.9 and following proof/discussion; PDF p. 20
his_places: Part D(i); Raptis bounded model structures
notes: Known existence route; explicit bounded cardinal construction is D.1.

statement: V ms.~37--44: the permissible replacements: The formal propositions on V ms.~37--42 remain theorems with the adjunction hypothesis in A.3--A.4. Their specialization to a right adjoint of $\varphi$ is refuted by B.4. For an individual category $K$, a local category weakly equivalent to $K$ exists if and only if $BK$ is a 1-type; in that case $\eta_K:K\to\Pi_1K$ is such a weak equivalence. For arbitrary $K$, a Thomason fibrant replacement exists, with the mapping property of A.5. For a fixed bounded family of sources, D.1 gives a target that represents the required Hom-functor on that family. For a weak-equivalence-invariant ind-represented functor, A.7 gives its descended ind-object in $\Hot$ without any envelope.
where_proved: sections/E.tex, statement E.1 and following proof/discussion; PDF p. 21
uses: CATHOT:A.3, CATHOT:A.4, CATHOT:A.5, CATHOT:A.7, CATHOT:B.4, CATHOT:C.3, CATHOT:D.1

statement: V ms.~45: the uniform-stage lemma: Let $K_0\subset K_1\subset\cdots$ be full subcategories with union $K_\infty$. If $X$ has finitely many objects, with no restriction on its number of arrows, the canonical comparison is an isomorphism of categories \[ \colim_n\Fun(X,K_n)\longrightarrow\Fun(X,K_\infty), \] and therefore a bijection on components. For an arbitrary filtered diagram of categories the same conclusion holds if $X$ has finitely many arrows. Neither conclusion identifies $\pi_0\Fun(X,K_\infty)$ with $[BX,BK_\infty]$ without an additional argument.
where_proved: sections/E.tex, statement E.2 and following proof/discussion; PDF p. 21

statement: V ms.~43 and 46: what fibrant replacement and filtered union supply: An actual sequence $K_n\to K_{n+1}$ admits a strictly commuting map to a sequence of Thomason-fibrant categories $R_n$ with each $K_n\to R_n$ a trivial cofibration. Its induced map of filtered colimits is in $\W_\infty$. Filtered colimits of Thomason-fibrant categories are Thomason-fibrant. In contrast, filtered unions of local categories need not be local, even with finite full stages.
where_proved: sections/E.tex, statement E.3 and following proof/discussion; PDF p. 22

statement: V ms.~47--49: an ind-isomorphism need not induce a weak equivalence of unions: There are finite full filtrations $T_0\subset T_1\subset\cdots$, every $T_n$ local and Thomason-fibrant, with fibrant union $T$, and functors $s,\id_T:T\rightrightarrows T$ such that they induce the same morphism of $(T_n)$ in $\Ind(\Cathot)$, but $Bs$ is not a weak equivalence and is not homotopic to the identity. Thus even the additional fibrancy of every stage and both unions does not rescue either the union-isomorphism inference or the uniqueness question of V ms.~47--49.
where_proved: sections/E.tex, statement E.4 and following proof/discussion; PDF p. 22
notes: Finite full stages local and fibrant; union fibrant but nonlocal. Independent local-union hypothesis is treated in E.18.

statement: V ms.~48: a local target does not force a strict retract: Even when $A$ is local, $i:A\hookrightarrow B$ is a Thomason cofibration, and a functor $p:B\to A$ satisfies $[p][i]=\id_A$ in $\Cathot$, there need not exist any functor $r:B\to A$ with $ri=\id_A$ as an equality in $\Cat$.
where_proved: sections/E.tex, statement E.5 and following proof/discussion; PDF p. 23
notes: Exhaustive 729-map check; target is local but not Thomason-fibrant.

statement: The additional fibrancy version of strict retraction: For a Thomason-fibrant category $A$, a Thomason cofibration $i:A\hookrightarrow B$, and a functor $p:B\to A$ with $[p][i]=\id_A$ in $\Cathot$, this audit does not decide whether some strict retraction $r$ exists in the same $\Cathot$ class as $p$. The finite example in E.5 does not satisfy this extra fibrancy hypothesis.
where_proved: sections/E.tex, statement E.6 and following proof/discussion; PDF p. 23
notes: Strict retraction in the same Hot class is proved; preservation of the original Cathot class remains undecided.

statement: V ms.~49--52: categorical homotopy and a canonical mapping object: Stagewise natural-transformation homotopies do not imply a global one, even with full fibrant filtrations, by E.4. Without fibrancy the fence of C.5 realizes the manuscript's proposed unbounded-length mechanism. Fibrancy also does not make every categorical homotopy a single transformation. A canonical replacement for arbitrary relative-category mapping types is a derived mapping space of the simplicial localization, whose components are the localized Hom-sets; this construction has no right adjoint $\Hot\to\Cathot$ as an input.
where_proved: sections/E.tex, statement E.7 and following proof/discussion; PDF p. 24

statement: VII ms.~108--124: total categories and actual filtered diagrams: For an actual filtered diagram $D:I\to\Cat$, the canonical map from its Grothendieck construction to $\colim_I D$ is a weak equivalence. Objectwise weak equivalences of actual filtered diagrams induce weak equivalences of colimits. If $P$ has finite CW type, then \[ \colim_i[P,BD_i]\longrightarrow[P,B\colim_iD_i] \] is a bijection. These conclusions do not follow from a mere isomorphism of the diagrams as ind-objects in $\Cathot$ or $\Hot$, and the last assertion is false for a general nerve of a finite category.
where_proved: sections/E.tex, statement E.8 and following proof/discussion; PDF p. 24

statement: External Hom in the rectified setting, with its size condition: Suppose a relative category $(\mathcal M,W)$ presents an $\infty$-category $\mathcal C$, and suppose, for every test category $X$ under consideration, its strict diagram localization presents the coherent diagram category: \[ \mathcal M^X[W_X^{-1}]\simeq h\Fun(NX,\mathcal C), \] naturally and compatibly with constant diagrams. Put $Z_{a,b}=\Map_{\mathcal C}(a,b)$. Then \[ \Hom_{\mathcal M^X[W_X^{-1}]}(a_X,b_X) \cong[BX,Z_{a,b}]. \] The derived mapping object $Z_{a,b}$, not a Thomason--Kan envelope, is the correct representing object on $\Hot$. If $\mathcal M$ is $\U$-small and the manuscript's countable path ind-representation holds on all $\Cat_\U$, then this additional rectification assertion on all those shapes forces each $Z_{a,b}$ to be a 1-type.
where_proved: sections/E.tex, statement E.9 and following proof/discussion; PDF p. 25
notes: Retains exact diagram-rectification and universe hypotheses.

statement: VII ms.~128--136: strict arrows, strict diagrams, and path types: For every category $C$, the canonical map \[ B\Fun([1],C)\longrightarrow\Map(B[1],BC) \] is a weak equivalence. Its strict fibre at $(a,b)$ need not be a homotopy fibre. For an arbitrary source $Y$, replacing $C$ by a Thomason-fibrant category does not make the corresponding comparison a weak equivalence, and it need not make $\Fun(Y,C)$ fibrant. A corrected mapping-space formula is $\Map_{\mathbf{sSet}}(NY,RNC)$, or the cosimplicial formula of A.5.
where_proved: sections/E.tex, statement E.10 and following proof/discussion; PDF p. 25
notes: Absolute arrow comparison is true; strict endpoint-fibre comparison can fail.

statement: VII ms.~127, 150--156 and IX ms.~13: what the set-valued arguments prove: An equality or an inverse verified only in $\Hot_0^{\wedge}$ cannot in general be pulled back to an equality or an inverse in $\Hot$. Thus the finite-test arguments for associativity, $T^2=1$, and weak equivalence of the displayed fibre-transition maps do not prove those conclusions. They are valid statements at the presheaf or ind-object level at which they were established. Fully coherent space-valued finite tests recover the conclusions, and height-two tests detect a specified weak equivalence. Equality of specified maps requires the stronger conditions detailed in Part F. For the actual all-arrows path construction, E.20 and following give direct proofs independent of these invalid inferences.
where_proved: sections/E.tex, statement E.11 and following proof/discussion; PDF p. 26
uses: CATHOT:E.20, CATHOT:E.4, CATHOT:F.13, CATHOT:F.2, CATHOT:F.6, CATHOT:F.7, CATHOT:F.9

statement: IX ms.~9--13: product-preserving passage and the second psi: The functors $\varphi$, their ind-extensions, restricted Yoneda $R_1^{\mathrm{cat}}$, and filtered-colimit realization in the presheaf category preserve finite products. They preserve the component sets obtained by evaluation at $e$. Therefore composition already specified as a morphism in one of these categories passes forward and gives the same ordinary category on components. The functor $R_1^{\mathrm{cat}}$, called $\psi$ on this page, is neither faithful, full, nor conservative. Its ind-extension is not faithful or full, since these failures already occur on constant ind-objects.
where_proved: sections/E.tex, statement E.12 and following proof/discussion; PDF p. 26

statement: IX ms.~10: nonconstant ind-objects can have ordinary colimits in Hot: The assertion that an ind-object of $\Hot$ can have a colimit there only when it is essentially constant is false. The finite discrete spaces $D_n=\{0,\ldots,n\}$ have the discrete countable space $\N$ as colimit in $\Hot$, although $(D_n)$ is not essentially constant in $\Ind(\Hot)$.
where_proved: sections/E.tex, statement E.13 and following proof/discussion; PDF p. 27

statement: IX ms.~22--23: the written tests permit a finite nontrivial relative category: There is a finite pointed relative category $(\mathcal E,W)$, whose localization is not equivalent to a point, satisfying the representability tests for $\Sigma,\Omega$, the weak-equivalence invariance of the constant-diagram external Hom, and the displayed higher loop-mapping formulas, when those tests are interpreted exactly as written before the finite-limit hypothesis of IX ms.~24. A finite pointed category with all finite products, by contrast, is necessarily equivalent to the terminal category.
where_proved: sections/E.tex, statement E.14 and following proof/discussion; PDF p. 27
notes: Five-arrow finite pointed example; finite products are a separate additional hypothesis.

statement: IX ms.~22--25: representability versus derived loops: In a pointed $\infty$-category $\mathcal C$ having the required finite limits and colimits, define $\Omega b=0\times_b^h0$ and $\Sigma a=0\amalg_a^h0$. There are canonical pointed equivalences \[ \Map_{\mathcal C}(a,\Omega b)\simeq \Omega\Map_{\mathcal C}(a,b)\simeq \Map_{\mathcal C}(\Sigma a,b), \] compatible with loop multiplication. They give $\Sigma\dashv\Omega$ on the homotopy category. In a pointed simplicial model category they can be calculated by replacing $b$ by a fibrant object and factoring its diagonal as \[ b\xrightarrow{\simeq}P b\xrightarrow{(d_0,d_1)}b\times b, \] with the second arrow a fibration, then taking the fibre at the zero pair. The first arrow must be a weak equivalence; merely calling it a cofibration is insufficient.
where_proved: sections/E.tex, statement E.15 and following proof/discussion; PDF p. 28

statement: V ms.~44 and 46: local presentations of invariant ind-objects: The following sequential assertion remains unresolved in this audit. Let $K=(K_n)_{n\in\N}$ be a sequence in $\Cathot_\U$, and assume that its associated presheaf \[ H_K(X)=\colim_n\Hom_{\Cathot}(X,K_n) \] sends every map in $\W_\infty$ between $\U$-small categories to a bijection. Must $K$ be isomorphic in $\Ind_\U(\Cathot_\U)$ to a sequence of local categories, equivalently to a sequence of groupoids? The corresponding assertion with an arbitrary $\U$-small filtered indexing category in place of $\N$ also remains unresolved here. We do not infer either assertion from descent in A.7, from the representable-object classification in Part C, or from the obstruction in D.8 for a single represented homotopy type.
where_proved: sections/E_ind.tex, statement E.17 and following proof/discussion; PDF p. 30
uses: CATHOT:A.4, CATHOT:A.7, CATHOT:C.3, CATHOT:C.4, CATHOT:D.7, CATHOT:D.8, CATHOT:E.4
notes: Exact proved criterion is invariance under every unit X→Pi1X, equivalently ind-unit isomorphism, with same-index groupoid presentation. W-infinity invariance implies this criterion remains unresolved. Proved for cofinally1-type stages or representable descended presheaf. Enlarged V-small index version is false by D.7.

statement: V ms.~47--49 with genuinely local unions: Let $(K_n)$ and $(K'_n)$ be sequences of full inclusions of $\U$-small categories, with unions $K,K'$. Suppose that the unions themselves are local. Let $u:K\to K'$ be an actual functor carrying each $K_n$ into some $K'_{m(n)}$. If the induced morphism in $\Ind_\U(\Cathot_\U)$ is invertible, then $[u]$ is invertible in $\Cathot$. If two such functors $u,v:K\rightrightarrows K'$ induce the same ind-morphism, then $[u]=[v]$ in $\Cathot$. Localness of the unions is a separate hypothesis here; it does not follow from localness of the stages.
where_proved: sections/E_local_union.tex, statement E.18 and following proof/discussion; PDF p. 31

statement: A coherent replacement for arbitrary relative path composition: Let $\mathcal M$ be $\U$-small and let $W$ be a subcategory containing every object. The hammock localization, followed on each mapping simplicial set by $\operatorname{Ex}^{\infty}$, gives $\U$-small Kan complexes \[ \mathcal H_W(a,b)=\operatorname{Ex}^{\infty} L^H(\mathcal M,W)(a,b) \qquad(a,b\in\mathcal M) \] with strictly associative, strictly unital simplicial composition. Their component category is canonically $\mathcal M[W^{-1}]$. Precomposition or postcomposition by any specified arrow in $W$ is a weak equivalence of these mapping complexes. These are coherent mapping objects for the relative localization. No comparison with a specified ordinary colimit of the manuscript's path categories is part of this assertion.
where_proved: sections/E_derived.tex, statement E.19 and following proof/discussion; PDF p. 32

statement: Finite support and the constant-path equivalence: The constant-path section $j:X\to\mathcal P(X)$ is a weak equivalence. For each $a\in X$, both one-endpoint categories $\mathcal P(X;a,?)$ and $\mathcal P(X;?,a)$ are weakly contractible.
where_proved: sections/E_path.tex, statement E.20 and following proof/discussion; PDF p. 33
depends_on: Explicit finite interval contraction; filtered colimits of nerves
notes: Sigma is all arrows; no contraction of a two-endpoint fibre is claimed

statement: The exact endpoint fibres are homotopy fibres: For each $a,b\in X$, the natural square \[ \begin{array}{ccc} B\mathcal P(X;a,b)&\longrightarrow&B\mathcal P(X)\\ \downarrow&&\downarrow Bp\\ \{(a,b)\}&\longrightarrow&K\times K \end{array} \] is homotopy Cartesian. In particular $B\mathcal P(X;a,b)$ has the weak homotopy type of the ordinary path space $P_{a,b}K$. The comparison with the homotopy fibre is natural for functors over $X\times X$.
where_proved: sections/E_path.tex, statement E.21 and following proof/discussion; PDF p. 34
depends_on: E.20; Quillen A and B; positive even-even and odd-odd support intervals; E.20; Quillen1973; Shoikhet2016
notes: Both lift tests and the two comma-projection variances are proved explicitly

statement: The actual even translation is the identity in the homotopy category: Let $T^2:\mathcal P(X)\to\mathcal P(X)$ be given by $(T^2c)(j)=c(j-2)$, with the corresponding shift on arrows and on natural transformations. It induces the identity in $\Hot$ on the total category and on every fixed-endpoint category.
where_proved: sections/E_path.tex, statement E.22 and following proof/discussion; PDF p. 35
notes: Cancellation of the constant-path equivalence in the localized slice; derived fibres identify the exact map

statement: The one-sided models and their actual comparison maps: Put $D=(+,-)$. Let $\mathcal L(X)$ be the colimit of the categories of $D^n$-paths under padding by a constant $D$-block on the left, and let $\mathcal R(X)$ use padding on the right. They have constant-path sections and endpoint maps. Their constant-path sections are weak equivalences, their one-endpoint fibres are weakly contractible, and their strict two-endpoint fibres compute their derived endpoint fibres. Constant-tail extension gives functors \[ q_L:\mathcal L(X)\longrightarrow\mathcal P(X), \qquad q_R:\mathcal R(X)\longrightarrow\mathcal P(X) \] which are weak equivalences on total categories and on every fixed-endpoint fibre. These comparisons commute with the canonical path-space comparisons of E.21.
where_proved: sections/E_path.tex, statement E.23 and following proof/discussion; PDF p. 35
depends_on: E.20-E.21; explicit identity-collar sliding homotopy; finite-support translation; E.20; E.21; Shoikhet2016
notes: Independent proof for actual half-fence colimits; Shoikhet2016 Proposition 3.3 is a related source and not a required identification

statement: The manuscript's left-right concatenation is associative: For the block $D=(+,-)$ and $\Sigma=\Mor(X)$, glue a left-half path and a right-half path at their common value at zero. This is an actual functor \[ \kappa:\mathcal L(X)\times_X\mathcal R(X)\longrightarrow\mathcal P(X), \] where the pullback uses the terminal and initial endpoints. On fixed fibres define the manuscript's composition by \[ \mu_{a,b,c}=B\kappa\,\bigl((Bq_L)^{-1}\times(Bq_R)^{-1}\bigr): B\mathcal P(X;a,b)\times B\mathcal P(X;b,c) \longrightarrow B\mathcal P(X;a,c) \quad\hbox{in }\Hot. \] Here the inverses refer to the fixed-fibre weak equivalences of E.23. Under the canonical comparisons to ordinary path spaces, this \emph{particular} operation is ordinary path concatenation. It is therefore associative and unital in $\Hot$; reversal supplies inverses in the usual path-groupoid sense, and the loop object is a group object of $\Hot$.

statement: Canonical relative collars and literal even translation: For any admissible $\Sigma$, let $\mathcal L_\Sigma(X;a,b)$, $\mathcal R_\Sigma(X;a,b)$, and $\mathcal P_\Sigma(X;a,b)$ be the full relative subcategories of the canonical $D=(+,-)$ models of E.23. The actual constant-tail extension maps $q_L,q_R$ are weak equivalences on these fibres and on their total categories. The literal translation $(T^2c)(j)=c(j-2)$ induces the identity in $\Hot$ on every such fibre. Gluing with the inverses of $q_L,q_R$ consequently defines the canonical relative operation $\mu_D$ in $\Hot$; constant paths are its left and right units.

statement: The remaining cofinal-type and all-type comparisons: For arbitrary admissible $\Sigma$ and arbitrary left-cofinal projective type sequences as just defined, this audit leaves undecided the following \emph{specified geometric} assertions of VII ms.~108--123: \begin{enumerate} \item A natural transformation $u:t\to t'$ of projective sequences, consisting of strictly commuting maps $u_n:t_n\to t'_n$, always induces a weak equivalence \[ u^*:C_{\infty,\Sigma}(t';a,b)\longrightarrow C_{\infty,\Sigma}(t;a,b). \] \item The isomorphisms obtained from the canonical type projections $t*t'\to t,t'$ are independent of all comparison choices and form the transitive canonical system asserted at ms.~119--123. \item The manuscript's comparison from a sequential colimit to its \emph{all-type} path category is an isomorphism in $\Hot$ for every such relative datum. Precisely, let $E_t$ be the fibred Grothendieck construction of the displayed sequence over $\N^{\op}$ and let $\mathrm{Ch}_\Sigma(X;a,b)\to\mathrm{Ty}$ have fibre $\Fun_\Sigma(I_\tau,X)_{a,b}$. The assertion is that \[ E_t\longrightarrow\mathrm{Ch}_\Sigma(X;a,b) \] is a weak equivalence, so that the span with the ordinary-colimit comparison $E_t\to C_{\infty,\Sigma}(t;a,b)$ yields the claimed isomorphism. \end{enumerate}

Denote their colimits by $L_{\tau_0,\Sigma}$, $R_{\tau_0,\Sigma}$, and $P_{\tau_0,\Sigma}$, with endpoints understood. Constant padding defines actual maps $q_L:L_{\tau_0,\Sigma}\to P_{\tau_0,\Sigma}$ and $q_R:R_{\tau_0,\Sigma}\to P_{\tau_0,\Sigma}$, and concatenation defines the actual gluing functor $\kappa_{\tau_0}$. statement: The two relevant finiteness conditions: Every finite CW homotopy type is represented by a finite poset. A category with finitely many arrows has a nerve with a finite $2$-skeleton, so each component of its classifying space has finitely presented fundamental group. Its nerve need not be homotopy equivalent to a finite CW complex. In particular the one-object category $BC_2$, with arrows $1,g$ and $g^2=1$, is finite, whereas $B(BC_2)$ is not a compact object of $\Spc$.

The compact objects of $\Spc$ are exactly the retracts in $\Spc$ of finite CW homotopy types; no assertion that all such retracts have finite CW type is needed.

statement: A precise gain for countable sources: Let $X$ have countable CW homotopy type, let $Y$ be any $\U$-small space, let $n\geq1$, and use finite CW tests. The canonical map \[ \theta_n:\tau_{\leq n-1}\Map(X,Y) \longrightarrow \Map_{\mathcal P_{n-1}(\mathcal A_{\mathrm{fin}})} (R_n^{\mathrm{fin}}X,R_n^{\mathrm{fin}}Y) \] is surjective on components. It induces isomorphisms on $\pi_k$ for $0\leq k<n-1$ and surjections on $\pi_{n-1}$, with basepoints wherever required. In particular coherent height-two finite CW tests determine equality of homotopy classes of maps with countable CW source. The same conclusion about equality holds if one is given coherent tests on all finite-category homotopy types.

statement: What testing can justify for composition and reversal: Let $P$ be a space with a specified morphism $m:P\times P\to P$ in $\Hot$, and let $T:P\to P$ be a specified endomorphism. Equality of the two associativity composites, or of $T^2$ and $\id_P$, does not follow in general from equality after every finite set-valued test. For each fixed finite height there are actual operations and endomorphisms for which the corresponding coherent finite-test identities hold but these identities in $\Hot$ fail. A coherent homotopy of their space-valued finite-test natural transformations does imply the corresponding equality in $\Hot$. A coherent height-two finite-test homotopy suffices when the source of the proposed equality has countable CW homotopy type. For arbitrary sources no fixed finite height supplies a general equality criterion: F.12 gives distinct ordinary homotopy classes with coherently identical finite tests at every prescribed finite height.

statement: Finite posets and necessary finiteness conditions: A homotopy type is the classifying-space type of a finite poset if and only if it has a finite CW model. Every homotopy type with a finite CW model consequently has a finite categorical model. For any finite category $C$, $BC$ has finitely many cells in each dimension, finitely many components, finitely presented fundamental groups, and finitely generated integral homology in every degree. These latter conditions do not imply that $BC$ has a finite CW model.

statement: The exact arrow-groupoid comparison and the pinning restriction Let $\sigma\supseteq\tau$, put $S_{\sigma,\tau}=\Stab(\sigma)\cap\Stab(\tau)$, and let $a=[1]:\sigma\to\tau$ be the associated exit arrow. The induced maps of the remaining labels must have the incidences specified in the definition of a normalization morphism; this is checked directly on the surviving half-edges. When these tests hold, $\bar j$ is unique, and the associated normalization and relative generization groupoids form a commuting square up to a canonical isomorphism. The comparisons are coherent under further admissible compositions. An unrestricted such square for every pair is false, already for the strict normalization and smoothing of the single loop in type $(1,1)$.
notes: Finite criterion for a normalization-contraction square; single-loop counterexample to an unrestricted square.

statement: The framed torsor and its two quotients For a pinned stable graph $G$, put \[ P_G=\prod_{j\in J(G),\,M_G} U(L_j),\qquad L_i=T_{x_i}C\quad(i\in I(G)),\qquad L_e=T_{x_h}C_{v(h)}\otimes T_{x_{\bar h}}C_{v(\bar h)}. \] Here $U(L)=L^{\times}/\mathbb R_{>0}$ is the oriented unit-ray circle bundle; no Hermitian metric is required. We write $P_G^E=\prod_{e\in E(G)}U(L_e)$. Choose a finite set $B_G$ in the pinned stratum, a nonempty finite set of rays above each member of $B_G$, and saturate the rays under $\mu_G=\{\pm1\}^{J(G)}$. Denote the resulting finite set by $D_G$. When a graph action is required, take $B_G$ invariant and also saturate $D_G$ under the finite group $\operatorname{Aut}(G)$. For vertices of genus zero and valence three or four, the groupoid \[ \mathcal S_G:=\Pi_1(P_G,D_G) \] is a $\mu_G$-free $\mathbb Z^{J(G)}$-groupoid, and its internal lattice acts freely on every nonempty Hom-set. Its geometric quotients are \[ \mathcal S_G/(\mathbb Z^{I(G)},\mu_2^{I(G)}) \simeq\Pi_1(P_G^E,\operatorname{im}D_G), \qquad \mathcal S_G/(\mathbb Z^{J(G)},\mu_G) \simeq\Pi_1(M_G,B_G). \tag{B.1} \] The first groupoid has the node-framed link group of Part A. The second has automorphism group $\prod_{v:\,|F_v|=4}F_2$. After choices of trivializations, the automorphism group of $\mathcal S_G$ is \[ \mathbb Z^{J(G)}\times\prod_{v:\,|F_v|=4}F_2. \tag{B.2} \] The direct-product splitting in (B.2) is not specified as $\operatorname{Aut}(G)$-equivariant.
notes: Topological circle bundles, labelled pinned rational components; graph action obtained by invariant finite ray saturation. Exact flag-to-edge tensor map and both lattice/sign quotients.

statement: The presentation actually written in scans 115--117 For a trivalent rational graph set $r=|J(G)|$. The finite model of cote 146, scans 114--117 (folios 113--116), has the $2^r$ objects of the sign torsor $D_G=\prod_{j\in J(G)}\varepsilon_j$. It has $r2^r$ positive half-turn generators \[ u_{j,x}:x\longrightarrow\sigma_jx \quad(j\in J(G),\ x\in D_G). \] Its relations are the source-compatible commuting squares for two different coordinates. The commutation of the full-turn loops $v_{j,x}=u_{j,\sigma_jx}u_{j,x}$ written on scan 117 follows from these squares. Equivalently, \[ \operatorname{Hom}(x,y)= \{m\in\mathbb Z^r:m\bmod2=y-x\}, \tag{B.4} \] where addition gives composition and $m$ records displacement in units of a half turn. The loop lattice is $2\mathbb Z^r$, identified with $\mathbb Z^r$ by $2e_j\mapsto e_j$.
notes: The coordinate half-turn presentation has 2^r objects, r·2^r positive generators and commuting squares. Half-turn squares are full meridians.

The groups of the unit tangent-ray bundles at all marked points are respectively \[ H_{1,1}=\langle a,b\mid aba=bab\rangle, \qquad z_1=(ab)^6, \tag{B.10} \] and \[ H_{1,2}=\left\langle a,b,c,z_1,z_2\ \middle|\ \begin{array}{l} aba=bab,\ bcb=cbc,\ ac=ca,\\ z_1,z_2\text{ central},\ (abc)^4=z_1z_2 \end{array}\right\rangle \cong B_4\times\mathbb Z. \tag{B.11} \] Here $z_i$ is the positive full turn at the $i$th marked point. The capping maps are the quotients $z_i\mapsto1$.

statement: All boundary graph groups in these two types For $(1,1)$ there is one boundary graph: a rational vertex with one loop and one labelled leg. Its pinned stratum is a point and its mixed stratum is $BC_2$. Put $h=(ab)^3$. Its fully framed mixed link group is \[ \langle a,h\mid[a,h]=1\rangle,\qquad z_1=h^2. \tag{B.12} \] Its node-only mixed link group is $\langle a,h\mid[a,h]=1,h^2=1\rangle$. For $(1,2)$ name the four boundary graph types as follows: $N$ is a rational vertex with a loop and both legs; $T$ is an elliptic vertex joined to a rational tail carrying both legs; $C$ is a two-edge rational cycle with one labelled leg on each vertex; and $D$ is a rational loop vertex joined to a rational tail carrying both legs. Write \[ s=aba,\quad\Delta=abcaba,\quad r=s^{-1}\Delta s,\quad q=(abc)^2,\quad h=(ab)^3, \quad d=h^2. \tag{B.13} \] The pinned stratum groups are $F_2$, $\operatorname{SL}_2(\mathbb Z)$, $1$, $1$ for $N,T,C,D$, respectively. The mixed stratum groups are $C_2*\mathbb Z$, $\operatorname{SL}_2(\mathbb Z)$, $C_2$, $C_2$. The following are presentations of their fully framed mixed link groups; in every row $z_1,z_2$ are central: \[ \begin{array}{c|l|l} \text{graph}&\text{generators and additional relations} &\text{node twists}\\\hline N&a,c,r,z_1,z_2;\ [a,c]=[a,r]=1,\ r^2=z_1z_2&a\\ T&a,b,z_1,z_2;\ aba=bab&d=(ab)^6\\ C&a,c,q,z_1,z_2;\ [a,c]=1,\ qaq^{-1}=c,\ q^2=z_1z_2&a,c\\ D&a,h,z_1,z_2;\ [a,h]=1&a,d=h^2 \end{array} \tag{B.14} \] The pinned full-framing subgroups are the kernels of the graph permutation: in rows $N,C,D$ the respective quotient maps send $r,q,h$ to the nonidentity member of $C_2$, and all lattice coordinates to the identity. The graph group in row $T$ is trivial. The node-only link groups are obtained by $z_1=z_2=1$. The mixed stratum groups are obtained by also killing the listed node twists.

statement: Finite chamber arrows reduced to pure moduli generators Let $m\geq3$. Its finite counts are \[ \begin{array}{c|r|r|r|r} \text{space}&\text{objects}&\text{arrows}& \text{rank-two relations}&\text{central relation}\\\hline M_{0,4}&6&12&6&1\\ M_{0,5}&24&72&72&1\\ M_{0,6}&120&480&720&1. \end{array} \tag{B.26} \] Every generator has an explicit image in the generators \[ A_{ij}=\sigma_{j-1}\cdots\sigma_{i+1}\sigma_i^2 \sigma_{i+1}^{-1}\cdots\sigma_{j-1}^{-1}, \qquad 1\leq i<j\leq m,\quad (i,j)\ne(1,2). \tag{B.27} \] The algorithm below and \texttt{b\_genus\_zero.json} specify all these words for $m=3,4,5$, and give the inverse on every generator by (B.27). Then $\Gamma_{0,6}=F(p,q,r,s)\rtimes\Gamma_{0,5}$, with the six relations (B.30) and the twenty equations $huh^{-1}=\phi_h(u)$ in the following table: \begingroup\small\setlength{\arraycolsep}{3pt} \[ \begin{array}{c|cccc} h&\phi_h(p)&\phi_h(q)&\phi_h(r)&\phi_h(s)\\\hline a&r^{-1}pr&c(p,r)q c(p,r)^{-1}&c(p,r)r&s\\ b&p&r^{-1}qr&c(q,r)r&s\\ x&s^{-1}ps&c(p,s)q c(p,s)^{-1}&c(p,s)r c(p,s)^{-1}&c(p,s)s\\ y&p&s^{-1}qs&c(q,s)r c(q,s)^{-1}&c(q,s)s\\ z&p&q&s^{-1}rs&c(r,s)s \end{array} \tag{B.31} \] \endgroup These are exactly the generators and relations in the supplied EXIT\_ONE\_TYPE statements P5c2 and P5c3, with the comparison specified by the individual band words (B.27). statement: A geometric realization of the bipyramid--pyramid incidence Let $U=\mathbb A^1_{\mathbb C}\setminus\{2,-2\}$ and \[ q_\mu(z)=z^4-\mu z^2+1. \] The roots of $q_\mu$, together with the distinguished point $\infty$, define a family of five-pointed spheres with the involution $z\mapsto-z$. The parameter $\mu=0$ belongs to this family: its fibre is the square-pyramidal configuration. Thus the extra deletion of $0$ in cote 148, scan 39 (folio 38), does not follow from the moduli problem with the fourth-root frame specified on scans 37--38 (folios 36--37). There is the following explicit realization in $\Pi_1M_{0,5}$ of the sixty $f_{B,s}$ incidences of scan 31. In one labelling, put \[ K(r)=\bigl(\infty,-ir,ir,-1,1\bigr), \qquad \frac1{\sqrt3}\leq r\leq1. \tag{B.32} \] Its initial configuration is bipyramidal and its final configuration is square-pyramidal. Relabelling (B.32) gives sixty paths, with twenty initial objects, thirty final objects, three paths leaving each initial object and two arriving at each final object. The endpoint functors are exactly \[ \begin{gathered} \mathfrak S_5/H_B \longleftarrow \mathfrak S_5/H \longrightarrow \mathfrak S_5/H_Q,\\ H_B=\langle(012),(12)(34)\rangle,\quad H_Q=\langle(1324)\rangle,\quad H=\langle(12)(34)\rangle. \end{gathered} \tag{B.33} \] In particular these are the endpoint maps used in B.13, now furnished with actual paths. statement: A complete presentation on the sixty geometric core paths The fifty-object, sixty-arrow path diagram (B.32)--(B.33) has a quotient groupoid equivalent to $\Pi_1M_{0,5}$ by the following twelve relations. Its comparison functor sends every arrow to the path (B.32), with its specified relabelling. The construction below specifies all basepoint transports, eleven free graph cycles, their five-point braid words, and an inverse on the five standard generators. Number cosets of each group in (B.33) by the lexicographically least permutation in the coset, with the permutations written as tuples of images of $0,1,2,3,4$. Number the sixty arrows $E_1,\ldots,E_{60}$ in that order. Use the breadth-first spanning tree from the first bipyramidal vertex, inspecting incident arrows in their numerical order. Its non-tree arrows are \[ E_2,E_3,E_6,E_8,E_9,E_{13},E_{19},E_{22},E_{42},E_{45},E_{48}. \tag{B.35} \] If $t_v$ is the tree path from the root to $v$, the corresponding free cycles $g_j$ traverse $t_{s(E)}$, then $E$, then $t_{t(E)}^{-1}$. Their exact words are the following. A signed integer $k$ denotes $E_k$ for $k>0$ and $E_{-k}^{-1}$ for $k<0$; within each bracket the paths are traversed from left to right. \begingroup\small \[ \begin{array}{c|l} g_1 &[1,-12,41,-44,20,-17,50,-59,35,-26,2,-11,53,-56,33,-28,39,-46,23,-14]\\ g_2 &[1,-12,54,-55,21,-16,3,-10,52,-57,23,-14]\\ g_3 &[1,-12,41,-44,20,-17,6,-7,39,-46,23,-14]\\ g_4 &[1,-12,54,-55,34,-27,8,-5,49,-60,36,-25]\\ g_5 &[1,-12,41,-44,31,-30,9,-4,38,-47,36,-25]\\ g_6 &[1,-12,41,-44,20,-17,50,-59,35,-26,13,-24,58,-51,30,-31,44,-41,12,-1]\\ g_7 &[14,-23,57,-52,29,-32,19,-18,49,-60,36,-25]\\ g_8 &[14,-23,46,-39,28,-33,22,-15,38,-47,36,-25]\\ g_9 &[14,-23,46,-39,28,-33,56,-53,42,-43,32,-29,52,-57,23,-14]\\ g_{10}&[1,-12,41,-44,31,-30,51,-58,45,-40,27,-34,55,-54,12,-1]\\ g_{11}&[1,-12,41,-44,20,-17,50,-59,48,-37,16,-21,55,-54,12,-1]. \end{array} \tag{B.36} \] \endgroup With the transport to the normalized configuration $(0,1,10,20,\infty)$ specified in the proof, their images in the presentation (B.30) are \[ \begin{array}{c|l@{\qquad}c|l} g_1&abyz&g_2&z\\ g_3&abz&g_4&z^{-1}y^{-1}z\\ g_5&axz&g_6&z^{-1}x^{-1}z\\ g_7&z^{-1}xz&g_8&b^{-1}z^{-1}y^{-1}\\ g_9&b^{-1}a^{-1}z^{-1}y^{-1}x^{-1}&g_{10}&abxyz\\ g_{11}&a&&. \end{array} \tag{B.37} \] Define words in these cycles by \[ A=g_{11},\qquad B=g_{11}^{-1}g_3g_2^{-1},\qquad X=g_2g_6^{-1}g_2^{-1},\qquad Y=g_2g_4^{-1}g_2^{-1},\qquad Z=g_2. \tag{B.38} \] The first six defining relations are \[ \begin{array}{lll} g_1=g_3g_4^{-1},&g_5=g_{11}g_2g_6^{-1},&g_7=g_6^{-1},\\ g_8=g_2g_3^{-1}g_{11}g_4g_2^{-1},& g_9=g_2g_3^{-1}g_4g_6g_2^{-1},& g_{10}=g_3g_6^{-1}g_4^{-1}. \end{array} \tag{B.39} \] The remaining six, with $c(U,V)=V^{-1}U^{-1}VU$, are \[ \begin{array}{lll} AXA^{-1}=Z^{-1}XZ,& AYA^{-1}=c(X,Z)Yc(X,Z)^{-1},& AZA^{-1}=c(X,Z)Z,\\ BXB^{-1}=X,& BYB^{-1}=Z^{-1}YZ,& BZB^{-1}=c(Y,Z)Z. \end{array} \tag{B.40} \] All twelve are based at the root; their conjugates supply the relation at any other object. Formulas (B.36), (B.38)--(B.40) are a complete explicit system, with no additional unspecified relators.

statement: A strict finite colimit with the five elementary types Let $S$ be an oriented stable surface with individually labelled boundary circles $I$, let $H=\Gamma(S,\partial S)$, and put $A=\mathbb Z^I$, with its positive boundary-twist generators. There is a strict finite diagram of finite-object groupoids, with a free action of $\mu=A/2A$ on their object sets, whose ordinary colimit is equivalent to the fundamental groupoid of the full tangent-ray bundle of the corresponding moduli stack, restricted to the specified finite rays. The equivalence preserves the boundary half-turns and full turns. The pieces are obtained by cutting and sewing from the five types \[ (0,3),\quad(0,4),\quad(0,5),\quad(1,1),\quad(1,2). \tag{B.74} \] For genus zero the index can be the finite poset of reduced labelled trees $G$ with \[ \sum_v(\operatorname{val}(v)-3)\leq2, \] ordered by edge contraction. The local five-point and elliptic pieces here are the explicitly presented groupoids of B.19, B.25 and B.9--B.11. For a pinned graph with several vertices, finite products and the flag-to-edge induction of B.1 give the same result with the full external lattice $\mathbb Z^{E(G)\amalg I(G)}$. This proves a geometric finite-colimit recipe with all five pieces (B.74). It does not remove the elliptic pieces in favour of only three- and four-point sphere pieces, nor identify an unstated original finite ray convention. B.29--B.30 supply explicit sphere covering and path-map replacements; the individual manuscript assignment and ray conventions remain recorded in B.8 and B.15.

statement: The contact matrix and the functor of generization diagrams For every stable $(g,n)$, forgetting the last marked point induces \[ Q:\mathcal E_{g,n+1}\longrightarrow\mathcal E_{g,n}, \qquad \sigma\longmapsto q\sigma,\qquad[a]\longmapsto[\phi(a)], \] where $q$ removes peripheral curves and identifies curves becoming isotopic, and $\phi:\Gamma_{g,n+1}\twoheadrightarrow\Gamma_{g,n}$ is the forgetful homomorphism. It acts on graph objects by stabilization, on the pinned component moduli by forgetting and stabilizing, and on the relative and full angular-link groupoids by the induced homomorphisms of stabilizers. On their meridian lattices its only nonidentity blocks are \[ \begin{aligned} \Z&\longrightarrow0&&\text{(contracted rational tail)},\\ \Z^2&\longrightarrow\Z,\quad(u,v)\longmapsto u+v &&\text{(contracted rational bridge)}. \end{aligned} \] These homomorphisms commute with both arrows of (103), with every flag-composition map, and with relabelling. They give the effect at infinity proposed in the deleted section on cote 147, scan 105.

statement: The smooth/topological surface comparison actually used For a compact oriented surface with finitely many individually fixed points, the inclusion $\Diff^+(S;I)\to\Homeo^+(S;I)$ induces an isomorphism of component groups, compatible with forgetting points, cutting annuli, and the twist generators. For stable types their identity components are weakly contractible. The unstable identity-component homotopy types are $SO(3)$ for $(0,0)$, $S^1$ for $(0,1),(0,2)$, and the torus for $(1,0)$. These give, for tangent-framed punctures in the two spherical marked cases, the respective kernel maps \[ \Z\twoheadrightarrow0, \qquad \Z^2\twoheadrightarrow\Z^2/\langle(1,-1)\rangle. \] No stable-graph category of C.1 is assigned to these unstable types.

statement: Restriction to the open fibre and the automorphism comparison Let $U_r=\mathbb P^1(\mathbb C)\setminus\{r\text{ labelled points}\}$, $r\geq3$, and give $\mathbb P^1$ the stratification by those points and their complement. Its strict completed exit category has one open object with group $\widehat\pi_r=\widehat F_{r-1}$, $r$ closed objects with trivial groups, and crossing sets $\widehat\pi_r/I_i$, where $I_i$ is the peripheral procyclic subgroup. Restriction to the open object induces an isomorphism \[ \operatorname{Aut}_{\mathrm{eq},I}(\widehat{\Exit}(\mathbb P^1,r)) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \Out_I(\widehat\pi_r). \tag{C.3} \] The left group is autoequivalences modulo natural isomorphism, preserving the labelled closed objects; on both sides we impose the same common multiplier on the chosen positive inertia generators. Allowing permutation of the labels gives the corresponding permuting version. These fibre exit categories occur in the universal stable-curve functors. Formula (C.3) is the map relating LM3b's surface-group automorphisms to the completed categories in this paper.

statement: An explicit full-profinite filling kernel in every spherical size Let $r\geq3$, let $F=\widehat F(x,y_1,\ldots,y_{r-1})$, set $p=xy_1\cdots y_{r-1}$, and put $\bar F=F/\langle\!\langle x\rangle\!\rangle=\widehat F(y_1,\ldots,y_{r-1})$. Let $O_{r+1,x}$ consist of peripheral-preserving outer automorphisms of $F$ fixing the distinguished puncture $x$, with a common unit multiplier, and let $O_r$ be the analogous group on $\bar F$. Filling and normalized filling are continuous surjections \[ f_x:O_{r+1,x}\twoheadrightarrow O_r, \qquad\theta_x:O_{r+1,x}\twoheadrightarrow\Aut_I(\bar F). \] Let $K\cong\bar F$ be the point-pushing subgroup. Then \[ \ker f_x=Q_r\rtimes K,\qquad Q_r\ne1. \tag{C.4} \] The following word model specifies $Q_r$ without a kernel notation. Put $N=\langle\!\langle x\rangle\!\rangle$. Take tuples $(w_1,\ldots,w_{r-1},w_\infty)\in N^r$ satisfying \[ x\prod_{j=1}^{r-1}w_j^{-1}y_jw_j=w_\infty^{-1}p w_\infty, \tag{C.5} \] and the finite test that, in every finite quotient $F\twoheadrightarrow H$, the images of the following elements generate $H$: \[ x,\quad w_1^{-1}y_1w_1,\quad\ldots,\quad w_{r-1}^{-1}y_{r-1}w_{r-1}. \] Denote the substitution they define by $\alpha_w$. The product is \[ (w*v)_j=w_j\alpha_w(v_j),\qquad (w*v)_\infty=w_\infty\alpha_w(v_\infty). \] Quotient by simultaneous right multiplication of all $w_j,w_\infty$ by $x^a$, $a\in\widehat\Z$. With its quotient profinite topology this is $Q_r$. Thus (C.4)--(C.5) give, in particular, the kernels of the fillings $4\to3$ and $5\to4$ as explicit profinite groups.
his_places: Longue Marche; supplied LM3b B.4–B.6; Part C(c)

statement: What the three bridge groups contribute at $5\to4$ Under the point-pushing and fibre comparisons of C.6--C.7, the profinite completion of each of the three $B\Z$ vertex groups for $\overline M_{0,5}\to\overline M_{0,4}$ maps injectively into $K=\widehat\pi_1(U_4)$. Its image is the procyclic subgroup generated by pushing around the corresponding two-versus-two separating curve; the original $\Z$ has dense cyclic image in it. Their closed normal closure inside $K$ has quotient $C_2$. Their intersection with $Q_4$ is trivial. Thus their actual contribution to the filling kernel in (C.4) lies entirely in its geometric point-pushing factor. The extra factor $Q_3\ne1$ already occurs for $4\to3$, where C.2 gives no bridge group.

statement: The nonorientable comparison and real-equivariant representatives For a compact smooth nonorientable surface, the inclusion of diffeomorphisms into homeomorphisms induces an isomorphism of mapping-class groups, also with individually fixed marked points and boundary fixed pointwise. For a closed nonorientable surface $N_h$ with $h$ crosscaps, the unmarked identity components in both categories have homotopy types \[ SO(3)\quad(h=1),\qquad S^1\quad(h=2),\qquad *\quad(h\geq3). \] With one fixed point $N_1$ has identity component of weak homotopy type $S^1$; with at least two it is weakly contractible. For $N_2$ with at least one fixed point, and for $N_h$ with $h\geq3$ with any number of fixed points, it is weakly contractible. Let $\tau$ be a specified smooth orientation-reversing involution of an oriented compact surface, and retain a specified finite $\tau$-invariant marking. statement: Actual surviving fibres and higher completed connectivity Fix $g\geq2$. Set $P=\pi_1(S_{g,n-1})$ and let $I_i\leq P$ be the peripheral cyclic subgroup about the retained puncture $p_i$. statement: Every finite cyclic group occurs in the Torelli completion kernel Let $g\geq3$, let $G=\Gamma_{g,0}$, and write \[ \rho:G\longrightarrow B=\operatorname{Sp}(2g,\mathbb Z), \qquad I=\ker\rho, \qquad K_I=\ker(\widehat I\longrightarrow\widehat G). \tag{D.163} \] For every integer $m\geq2$ there is a continuous epimorphism \[ K_I\longrightarrow C_m. \tag{D.164} \] The maps in this construction are chosen separately for different $m$. D.53 supplies an additional compatible sequence. More precisely, there are a normal finite-index subgroup $H\lhd G$, its actual Torelli intersection $N=H\cap I$, and an $H$-invariant epimorphism $u:N\to C_m$ such that \[ \begin{gathered} N'=\ker u\lhd H,\qquad [N:N']=m,\qquad \overline{N'}^{\,\widehat H}=\overline N^{\,\widehat H},\\ u(N\cap L)=C_m\quad\text{for every finite-index }L\leq H. \end{gathered} \tag{D.165} \] In particular, the full profinite topology of $I$ is not the topology induced by $G$. The nonzero coefficient class $u\in H^1(N;C_m)$ is fixed by $H/N$ and cannot be killed by any ambient finite-index refinement. This is an explicit obstruction to applying the coefficient-killing step of D.49 to the Torelli sequence. It does not evaluate the colimit (D.159).

statement: The exact Torelli filtration of the remaining degree-two obstruction Let $g\geq3$, let $G=\Gamma_{g,0}$, and put $B=\operatorname{Sp}(2g,\mathbb Z)$, $I=\ker(G\to B)$ and $K=\ker(\widehat I\to\widehat G)$. The kernel $K$ is central in $\widehat I$. In particular the maps $\Phi,j$ of D.53 give an isomorphism of profinite groups \[ K\cong\ker(\Phi)\times\widehat{\mathbb Z}, \qquad (k,t)\longmapsto k\,j(t). \tag{D.178} \] Fix a finite abelian group $A$, regarded as a constant coefficient group on every subgroup of $G$ and $B$. The induced action on fibre cohomology below retains the conjugation action. For $H\lhd_fG$ set $N_H=H\cap I$ and $\Lambda_H=\rho(H)$, where $\rho:G\to B$ is the symplectic representation. Define \[ \mathcal E_G^j(A)=\varinjlim_{H\lhd_fG}H^j(H;A),\qquad T_A^{p,q}=\varinjlim_{H\lhd_fG} H^p\bigl(\Lambda_H;H^q(N_H;A)\bigr). \tag{D.179} \] The coefficient action in the second formula is the actual conjugation action from $1\to N_H\to H\to\Lambda_H\to1$. All transition maps are restriction on the base followed by restriction on the fibre coefficient. There is a natural first-quadrant spectral sequence \[ T_A^{p,q}\ \Longrightarrow\ \mathcal E_G^{p+q}(A), \qquad d_r:E_r^{p,q}\longrightarrow E_r^{p+r,q-r+1}, \qquad E_2^{p,q}=T_A^{p,q}. \tag{D.180} \] Writing $\mathcal E_B^p(A)$ for the corresponding restriction colimit over normal finite-index subgroups of $B$, its bottom row and two other terms are \[ T_A^{p,0}=\mathcal E_B^p(A),\qquad T_A^{0,1}\cong\operatorname{Hom}_{\rm cts}(K,A),\qquad T_A^{1,1}=0. \tag{D.181} \] The first differential induces an injection \[ \theta_A=d_2:\operatorname{Hom}_{\rm cts}(K,A) \lhook\joinrel\longrightarrow \mathcal E_B^2(A). \tag{D.182} \] Define the two groups and their actual differentials by \[ \begin{split} U_A&=\ker\bigl(d_2:T_A^{0,2}\longrightarrow T_A^{2,1}\bigr),\\ P_A&=\ker\bigl(d_3:U_A\longrightarrow\mathcal E_B^3(A)\bigr). \end{split} \tag{D.183} \] Here $U_A=E_3^{0,2}$ and the stated target of $d_3$ is exactly $E_3^{3,0}$, rather than a further unspecified quotient. There is a natural short exact sequence \[ 0\longrightarrow \frac{\mathcal E_B^2(A)}{\theta_A\operatorname{Hom}_{\rm cts}(K,A)} \xrightarrow{\ \mathrm{inf}\ } \mathcal E_G^2(A) \xrightarrow{\ \mathrm{res}\ }P_A \longrightarrow0. \tag{D.184} \] Together with D.51, its middle term is canonically $\varinjlim_{H\lhd_fG}\operatorname{Hom}(J_H,A)$, where $J_H=\ker[H_2(H;\mathbb Z)\to H_2(G;\mathbb Z)]$ and the transition maps are precomposition with the actual inclusion maps on $H_2$. Neither outer term of (D.184) is evaluated here.

statement: The arithmetic action on the Torelli kernel and its fixed quotient Use the groups $G,B,I,K$ of D.54. statement: Infinitely many arithmetic obstruction directions Let $g\geq3$, $B=\operatorname{Sp}_{2g}(\mathbb Z)$, and $L=\widehat B$, with full profinite completion. For a finite trivial $B$-module $A$ put \[ \mathcal E_B^j(A)= \varinjlim_{\Lambda\triangleleft_f B}H^j(\Lambda;A), \qquad\text{transition maps } \operatorname{res}. \tag{D.196} \] Conjugation gives the smooth $L$-action on this discrete group. For $A=\mathbb Z/n$, $n\geq2$, there is an exact sequence \[ \begin{split} 0&\longrightarrow H^2_{\mathrm{cts}}(L;A) \longrightarrow H^2(B;A) \longrightarrow \mathcal E_B^2(A)^L\\ &\xrightarrow{\ d_3\ }H^3_{\mathrm{cts}}(L;A) \longrightarrow H^3(B;A). \end{split} \tag{D.197} \] The first and last arrows are restriction along $B\to L$. There is an injective homomorphism of discrete $\mathbb Z/n$-modules \[ \iota_n:\bigoplus_{\mathbb N}\mathbb Z/n \lhook\joinrel\longrightarrow \mathcal E_B^2(\mathbb Z/n)^L. \tag{D.198} \] In particular, for every prime $\ell$, \[ \dim_{\mathbb F_\ell}\mathcal E_B^2(\mathbb F_\ell)^L =\dim_{\mathbb F_\ell}\mathcal E_B^2(\mathbb F_\ell) =\aleph_0. \tag{D.199} \] These are the arithmetic restriction colimits occurring in D.54, with the same maps. Their infinitude is the symplectic specialization of \citet[Theorems 3--4, proofs in Sections 4--5]{Root_Hill2019}; the proof below specifies the finite symplectic classes and the comparison. Let $K_I$ and $\Phi:K_I\twoheadrightarrow\widehat{\mathbb Z}$ be the actual kernel and epimorphism of D.53--D.55, and let $u_\ell=\operatorname{red}_\ell\Phi$. Then $\theta(u_\ell)\ne0$ is $L$-fixed and \[ \dim_{\mathbb F_\ell} \left(\mathcal E_B^2(\mathbb F_\ell)^L/ \mathbb F_\ell\theta(u_\ell)\right)=\aleph_0. \tag{D.200} \] The full transgression quotient in D.54 is reached by the quotient map \[ \mathcal E_B^2(\mathbb F_\ell)/ \mathbb F_\ell\theta(u_\ell) \twoheadrightarrow \mathcal E_B^2(\mathbb F_\ell)/ \theta\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{cts}}(K_I,\mathbb F_\ell). \tag{D.201} \] Its kernel is the image of $\theta\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{cts}}(K_I,\mathbb F_\ell)$ modulo $\mathbb F_\ell\theta(u_\ell)$. This image and D.54's fibre permanent cycles remain to be computed.

statement: Two integral arithmetic directions and the Torelli line Let $g\geq3$, let $B=\operatorname{Sp}_{2g}(\mathbb Z)$, and fix a prime $\ell$. Use the restriction colimits of (D.196) and put \[ M_{\ell,t}=\mathcal E_B^2(\mathbb Z/\ell^t),\qquad M_\ell=\varprojlim_t M_{\ell,t},\qquad \mathscr A=\operatorname{Sp}_{2g}(\mathbb A_f). \tag{D.215} \] The coefficient maps in this inverse limit are reduction. The arithmetic action on $M_{\ell,t}$ restricts to the action of $\widehat B\subset\mathscr A$ in D.56. Write $N_\ell=M_\ell^{\mathscr A}$. Then \[ N_\ell\cong\mathbb Z_\ell^2, \qquad N_\ell/\ell^tN_\ell\lhook\joinrel\longrightarrow M_{\ell,t}^{\mathscr A} \lhook\joinrel\longrightarrow M_{\ell,t}^{\widehat B}. \tag{D.216} \] The first isomorphism is an isomorphism of topological $\mathbb Z_\ell$-modules; the subsequent arrows are the actual coefficient reduction and inclusion of invariant subgroups. Their domains are $(\mathbb Z/\ell^t)^2$, and their transition maps are reduction. This rank calculation is the symplectic specialization of \citet[Theorem 6 and Section 6]{Root_Hill2019}. Let $K$ and $\Phi$ be exactly those of D.53--D.55, let $\Phi_\ell:K\to\mathbb Z_\ell$ be its $\ell$-component, and let $\theta_\ell$ be the inverse limit of D.54's finite coefficient injections. With $v_\ell=\theta_\ell(\Phi_\ell)$, \[ v_\ell\in N_\ell,\qquad N_\ell/\mathbb Z_\ell v_\ell\cong\mathbb Z_\ell. \tag{D.217} \] The quotient map is fixed by $\Phi$; its displayed isomorphism with $\mathbb Z_\ell$ depends on a choice of generator. More precisely, let $\xi_\ell\in M_\ell$ be obtained from the real universal-cover extension, restricted to $\operatorname{Sp}_{2g}(\mathbb Q)$ and then to $B$, with the central-generator convention of D.52. Then \[ 2v_\ell=-\xi_\ell. \tag{D.218} \] Rationally there is an exact sequence with its indicated maps \[ \begin{split} 0&\longrightarrow H^2(\operatorname{Sp}_{2g}(\mathbb Q);\mathbb Q_\ell) \xrightarrow{\ a\ }N_\ell\otimes\mathbb Q_\ell\\ &\xrightarrow{\ b\ } H^3(\mathfrak{sp}_{2g,\mathbb Q_\ell};\mathbb Q_\ell) \longrightarrow0. \end{split} \tag{D.219} \] Both end terms have dimension one, and the image of $a$ is exactly $\mathbb Q_\ell v_\ell$. For both maps, first localize each finite-$S$ edge sequence at $\ell$ and then take its inverse limit. The first arrow is induced by arithmetic restriction and the coefficient map. The second is induced by the degree-three edge map and the natural continuous-to-Lie-algebra comparison at each such level. At each finite coefficient level the quotient by the specified line in (D.216) maps to D.54's quotient by the full transgression image. The kernel of that last map is its intersection with the remaining transgression image. Equations (D.216)--(D.219) do not compute that intersection or D.54's fibre permanent cycles.

statement: All relative levels recover the primary Torelli kernel Use $G,B,I,K$ from D.54 and put $P=\widehat I$ and $C=\overline I\subset\widehat G$. Fix a prime $\ell$. For $H\triangleleft_fG$ define \[ \begin{gathered} N_H=I\cap H,\quad U_H=\widehat N_H\subset P,\quad C_H=C\cap\widehat H,\quad\Lambda_H=\rho(H),\\ R_H=O^\ell(U_H) =\ker(U_H\longrightarrow U_H^{(\ell)}),\qquad K_{H,\ell}=K/(K\cap R_H). \end{gathered} \tag{D.228} \] For a profinite group, $O^\ell$ is the intersection of the kernels of its continuous maps to finite $\ell$-groups; the superscript $(\ell)$ denotes its maximal pro-$\ell$ quotient. All inclusions in (D.228) are the actual finite-index completion maps. The relative pro-$\ell$ completion of $H$ over the full arithmetic completion $\widehat\Lambda_H$ is \[ \mathcal R_H^{\rm all} =\widehat H/O^\ell(C_H), \qquad 1\longrightarrow K_{H,\ell} \longrightarrow N_H^{(\ell)} \longrightarrow\mathcal R_H^{\rm all} \longrightarrow\widehat\Lambda_H\longrightarrow1. \tag{D.229} \] Here ``relative'' means the universal profinite quotient over the specified base whose kernel over that base is pro-$\ell$. The first map is induced by $K\subset U_H$. There is also an exact map to the completion over the $\ell$-adic arithmetic image. Let $\Lambda_{H,\ell}$ be the closure of $\Lambda_H$ in $\operatorname{Sp}_{2g}(\mathbb Z_\ell)$ and put $D_H=\ker(\widehat H\to\Lambda_{H,\ell})$. Then \[ \begin{gathered} \mathcal R_H^{\ell}=\widehat H/O^\ell(D_H),\qquad \mathcal R_H^{\rm all}\twoheadrightarrow\mathcal R_H^{\ell},\\ \ker(\mathcal R_H^{\rm all}\to\mathcal R_H^\ell) =O^\ell(D_H)/O^\ell(C_H). \end{gathered} \tag{D.230} \] The corresponding Torelli-fibre kernels are related by \[ \begin{split} 1\longrightarrow K_{H,\ell} &\longrightarrow \ker\bigl(N_H^{(\ell)}\to\mathcal R_H^\ell\bigr)\\ &\longrightarrow \frac{C_H\cap O^\ell(D_H)}{O^\ell(C_H)} \longrightarrow1. \end{split} \tag{D.231} \] Every arrow is induced by the original quotient maps. For $H'\subset H$ there is a canonical equivariant surjection $K_{H',\ell}\to K_{H,\ell}$. If $K_\ell$ denotes the canonical pro-$\ell$ factor of the abelian profinite group $K$, these maps give \[ K_\ell\xrightarrow{\sim}\varprojlim_{H\triangleleft_fG} K_{H,\ell}. \tag{D.232} \] This is an isomorphism of profinite groups with their $\widehat B$-actions. For every finite abelian $\ell$-primary group $A$ with trivial action, precomposition with the quotient maps gives \[ \operatorname{Hom}_{\rm cts}(K,A)^{\widehat B} =\varinjlim_H \operatorname{Hom}_{\rm cts}(K_{H,\ell},A)^{\widehat B}, \tag{D.233} \] and consequently \[ \operatorname{Hom}_{\rm cts}(K,\mathbb Z_\ell)^{\widehat B} =\varprojlim_t\ \varinjlim_H \operatorname{Hom}_{\rm cts} (K_{H,\ell},\mathbb Z/\ell^t)^{\widehat B}. \tag{D.234} \] The order of these two limits is part of the statement. For a fixed $H$, the exact left-hand part of the restriction sequence is \[ \begin{split} 0\longrightarrow \operatorname{Hom}_{\rm cts}(K_{H,\ell},\mathbb Z_\ell)^{\widehat B} &\longrightarrow \operatorname{Hom}_{\rm cts}(K,\mathbb Z_\ell)^{\widehat B}\\ &\longrightarrow \operatorname{Hom}_{\rm cts}(K\cap R_H,\mathbb Z_\ell)^{\widehat B}. \end{split} \tag{D.235} \] Thus the last displayed restriction is the exact obstruction for a specified invariant character at that fixed level. The fixed-level examples proved below show why centrality and invariance alone do not remove such a restriction. No upper bound from a unipotent or a relative completion is imported into (D.232)--(D.235).
