statement: The full pants section centralizers in LM4 D.74 For the normalized involution and three section classes of R1, every section has trivial centralizer in the full $F=\widehat F(x,y)$. Thus $N_E(S_i)=S_i$ for all three classes. The equation $f=h^{-1}\alpha(h)$ has exactly one solution in $F$, and that solution lies in $F'$. The extension $E=F\rtimes_\alpha C_2$ is real projective. If $\alpha\in\widehat{GT}_0$, the unique solution also satisfies $h\theta(h)=1$, where $\theta$ exchanges $x,y$.
depends_on: R1 (refereed); C.5–C.6; KZ 2007 Theorem 2; Haran 1993 Proposition 2.2
notes: Full profinite groups unless explicitly designated pro-p or procongruence.

statement: Negative torus section counts, cusp fusion and the centralizer in LM4 D.75 Let an outer involution of $F=\widehat F(x,y)$ preserve the commutator cusp $c=[x,y]$ with full multiplier $-1$. Its centre-free extension has a cusp-normalized splitting \[ E=F\rtimes\langle v\rangle, \qquad v^2=1,\qquad vcv^{-1}=c^{-1}. \] Write $A_2$ for its action on $H_1(F,\mathbb Z_2)$. If $A_2\not\equiv I\pmod2$ there is one section class and its geometric centralizer is trivial. If $A_2\equiv I\pmod2$ there are two classes: the cusp class has trivial geometric centralizer and the other has $\dim_{\mathbb F_2}H^1(C_F(w),\mathbb F_2)=1$. The two local cusp reflection classes are globally fused. In particular there is a unique $g\in F$ with $gvg^{-1}=cv$.
depends_on: C.5–C.6; KZ 2007 Theorem 2; specified global multiplier −1; C.18 proves global sign from dyadic sign
notes: Full profinite groups unless explicitly designated pro-p or procongruence.

statement: The specified section augmentation module in LM4 D.76 In the pants extension of C.7 choose one actual section $T_i=\langle t_i\rangle$ from each class, and put $R=\mathbb F_2[[E]]$. Then the compact left module \[ \Delta_T=\ker\left(\bigoplus_{i=0}^2 \mathbb F_2[[E/T_i]]\longrightarrow\mathbb F_2\right) \] is isomorphic to $R^2$. For each finite $E$-module $M$, $\dim\operatorname{Hom}_E(\Delta_T,M)=2\dim M$. For the specified identity-coset vectors $e_i$ and $H=\overline{\langle T_0,T_1,T_2\rangle}$, the distinct incidence map satisfies \[ \begin{split} d_T:R^2&\longrightarrow\Delta_T, \quad(r_1,r_2)\longmapsto r_1(e_1-e_0)+r_2(e_2-e_0),\\ \operatorname{coker}d_T&\cong \ker\bigl(\mathbb F_2[[E/H]]\longrightarrow\mathbb F_2\bigr). \end{split} \tag{C.9.1} \] Thus $d_T$ is invertible exactly when the chosen sections generate $E$; freeness of $\Delta_T$ alone does not imply that conclusion.
depends_on: C.7; full continuous coefficient modules; Shapiro
notes: Full profinite groups unless explicitly designated pro-p or procongruence.

statement: The proper three-section example of LM4 D.77 In the full profinite free product $E_0=C_2(a)\amalg C_2(b)\amalg C_2(d)$ put \[ x=ba,\quad y=da,\quad \delta=\operatorname{Ad}(a),\quad g=x[x,y]x^{-1},\quad Y=g y\delta(g)^{-1}. \] The orientation kernel is $F_0=\widehat F(x,y)$. The sections $a,b,gdg^{-1}$ represent its three section classes, yet generate a proper closed subgroup $H<E_0$. Its orientation kernel is $K=\overline{\langle x,Y\rangle}<F_0$, although its image in every $F_0^{(p)}$ is full. The incidence cokernel of C.9 has a five-dimensional finite quotient. The element $Y$ is not conjugate to any unit power of $y$.
notes: Full profinite groups unless explicitly designated pro-p or procongruence.

statement: The original negative transporter is homologically primitive In C.8 the transporter $g$ has primitive abelianization and generates the full fixed line of $F^{\mathrm{ab}}$. In the two-class case put $B=C_F(w)$ for the other section. Its homology image is exactly that line. There is a continuous epimorphism $\chi:E\to\widehat{\mathbb Z}$ with $\chi(g)=1$ and $\chi(B)=\widehat{\mathbb Z}$; one can choose $a\in B$ with $[a]=[g]$. Killing all torsion in $E$ gives precisely this torsion-free quotient. In the one-class case the torsion-free quotient is also $\widehat{\mathbb Z}$, but its primitive character takes $g$ to $2$.
depends_on: C.8; exact finite-cover maps; class-two dyadic quotient
notes: Full profinite groups unless explicitly designated pro-p or procongruence.

statement: The exact pro-odd-kernel conclusions of LM4 D.78 In the two-class situation of C.11, retain its actual $B=C_F(w)$, $T=\langle w\rangle$, $\chi$ and chosen $a\in B$. Put $A=\overline{\langle a\rangle}$ and $K=\ker(\chi|_B)$. Then \[ \dim H^1(B_0,\mathbb F_2)=1\quad(B_0\leq B\text{ open}), \qquad B=K\rtimes A, \qquad A\cong\widehat{\mathbb Z}, \tag{C.12.1} \] and $K$ is pro-odd. For every finite two-primary $B$-module $Q$, inflation gives \[ H^n(\widehat{\mathbb Z},Q^K)\cong H^n(B,Q), \tag{C.12.2} \] and restriction to $A$ is the map induced by $Q^K\hookrightarrow Q$, with $t$ acting on $Q$ as $a^t$. The invariant-surjectivity criterion is exactly C.3, and remains additional to these conclusions.
depends_on: C.6; C.8; C.11; full finite E-sets
notes: Full profinite groups unless explicitly designated pro-p or procongruence.

statement: The exact transporter and conjugacy reduction of LM4 D.75 For $\mu\in\widehat{\mathbb Z}^{\times}$ and $i\in\{0,1\}$ put $v_i=c^iv$. The unique solution of $[a,v_i]=c^\mu$ is \[ a_{\mu,0}=c^{(\mu-1)/2}g, \qquad a_{\mu,1}=c^{(\mu+1)/2}g^{-1}. \tag{C.13.1} \] The full peripheral conjugacy to the corresponding standard negative torus involution is equivalent to \[ \exists\mu\in\widehat{\mathbb Z}^{\times},\ i\in\{0,1\}: c^{-\mu}a_{\mu,i}\sim_F a_{\mu,i}. \tag{C.13.2} \] Existence in (C.13.2) is not asserted.
depends_on: C.5; C.8; C.11; exact peripheral generation test
notes: Full profinite groups unless explicitly designated pro-p or procongruence.

statement: The existence requested by prompt C.2 For every negative involution of the full punctured-torus loop-outer group, does (C.13.2) have a solution? C.8 and C.13 prove uniqueness of every individual commutator transporter and all claimed equivalences in LM4 D.75. They do not supply the additional conjugacy. An outside element in $C_E(a_{\mu,i})$ would solve it; absence of such elements for all full units and both parity labels would refute it. The equation remains a full profinite conjugacy problem, and generation in each maximal pro-$p$ quotient does not solve it, as C.10 illustrates for the related section-generation problem.
notes: Full profinite groups unless explicitly designated pro-p or procongruence.

statement: Prime-order lifting and full closed-surface primary faithfulness Every outer action of $C_p$ on the full free profinite group $\widehat F_2$ has an actual order-$p$ representative if its outer image has order $p$. For the full completed closed surface group $\Pi=\widehat{\pi_1(S_g)}$, $g\geq2$, the map \[ \operatorname{Aut}(\Pi)\longrightarrow \operatorname{GL}(H_1(\Pi,\mathbb Z_p)) \tag{C.15.1} \] is injective on finite $p$-subgroups. This second assertion concerns actual automorphisms, not outer automorphisms.
depends_on: Jarden 1982 Theorem 1.2; Morales 2024 Propositions 2.14–2.15; KZ 2007 Theorem 2
notes: Full profinite groups unless explicitly designated pro-p or procongruence.

statement: The order-three assertion of LM4 D.42 Every element of order three in the full three-cusp loop-outer group allowing cusp permutations has multiplier $1\in\widehat{\mathbb Z}^{\times}$.
depends_on: C.15; R1 (refereed); cyclic cover and filling comparison
notes: The order-three claim is proved here; C.23 now proves the complete finite-subgroup consequence.

statement: The primary fixed-group and cusp arguments needed for the quartic audit Let $a$ be an actual automorphism of order $p$ of a full free profinite group $F_r$ which induces the identity on $F_r^{(p)}$. Then $F_r\rtimes_a C_p$ has one $F_r$-conjugacy class of sections, and restriction gives \[ H^1(F_r,\mathbb F_p)\xrightarrow{\sim} H^1(C_{F_r}(a),\mathbb F_p). \tag{C.17.1} \] If $F_r$ is the group of a sphere with $r+1\geq3$ cusps and $a$ preserves each cusp class with $p$-adic multiplier one, then $a=1$. If $r=2$ and $a$ preserves the torus cusp, the same conclusion holds. In particular the homology representation of the full torus loop-outer group is injective on each finite $p$-subgroup at its $p$-adic coordinate.
depends_on: C.15; KZ 2007 Theorem 2; exact cusp/cover comparisons
notes: Full versus pro-p comparison maps retained.

statement: The global torus involution sign, with the Heisenberg comparison specified Every involution of the full torus loop-outer group has multiplier equal to its global dyadic sign, $1$ or $-1$. This proves the upstream sign assertion LM4 D.43 used in the negative-involution and quartic calculations.
depends_on: C.15; characteristic Heisenberg cover; Schrodinger matrices
notes: Full versus pro-p comparison maps retained.

statement: Positive torus sections, full primary square, and actual quartic lifting A positive torus involution acts as $-I$ on $H_1(F,\mathbb Z_p)$ for every prime $p$. Its centre-free full extension has three kernel-conjugacy classes of sections, each with $H^1(C_F(S),\mathbb F_2)=0$. Its cusp normalizer is torsion-free, and a labelled cusp lift $v$ satisfies $v^2=c^\kappa$ with $\kappa_2$ a unit. Every order-four outer torus action has an actual order-four lift. For such an action, $A_p^2=-I$ at every prime, $\lambda^2=1$, and $\lambda_2=1$. These are precisely the portions of LM4 D.46 and D.55 needed below.
depends_on: C.17–C.18; Jarden 1982 Lemma 2.1; Brown and Bockstein
notes: Full versus pro-p comparison maps retained.

statement: The actual dihedral quotient behind the quartic argument Let $\alpha$ be the actual quartic torus representative of C.19, $c=[X,Y]$, and $E=F\rtimes\langle s\rangle$. There is a unique nonzero invariant character $\chi:F\to C_2$. One can choose a discrete free basis $x,y$, with $[x,y]=c$, $\chi(x)=1$, $\chi(y)=0$, such that the full quotient \[ F/\overline{\langle\!\langle x^2,(xy)^2\rangle\!\rangle} =\widehat{\mathbb Z}\rtimes C_2 =\langle r,t\mid t^2=1,\ trt=r^{-1}\rangle, \qquad x\mapsto t,\quad y\mapsto r \tag{C.20.1} \] is $\alpha$-invariant. The induced action is \[ \bar\alpha(r)=r^{-\lambda},\quad \bar\alpha(t)=r^jt,\quad (1-\lambda)j=0, \quad j_2\in\mathbb Z_2^\times. \tag{C.20.2} \] At every negative odd coordinate $q$, this gives a specified quotient $\rho:F\to D_{2q}$ with $\rho\alpha=\rho$, $\rho(c)=r^{-2}$, and $q\equiv1\pmod4$. This independently proves the portion of LM4 D.68 needed for D.70.
depends_on: C.19; exact Schreier double cover; norm and presentation maps
notes: Full versus pro-p comparison maps retained.

statement: The integral square on the nontrivial rotation summand Use a negative coordinate and the specified quotient of C.20. Put $N=\ker\rho$, $R=\langle r\rangle\cong C_q$, $\beta=\alpha^2$, $\sigma=s^2$, $C=C_F(\sigma)$ and $C_0=C\cap N$. Then \[ \rho(C)=R,\qquad \dim H^1(C_0,\mathbb F_2)=q-1. \tag{C.21.1} \] The cover $N$ has type $(q,2)$. If $V_2=H^1(N,\mathbb Z_2)$, $e=q^{-1}\sum_{r'\in R}r'$ and $W_2=(1-e)V_2$, then \[ \operatorname{rank}W_2=2(q-1),\qquad \beta^*|_{W_2}=I. \tag{C.21.2} \] There are two section classes in $N\rtimes\langle\sigma\rangle$, represented by $\langle\sigma\rangle$ and $x\langle\sigma\rangle x^{-1}$, with normalizers $C_0\times\langle\sigma\rangle$ and its $x$-conjugate. This proves LM4 D.69, including its integral conclusion.
depends_on: C.19–C.20; exact deck modules; Brown and mod-four cochains
notes: Full versus pro-p comparison maps retained.

statement: The quartic multiplier assertion of LM4 D.70 Every order-four element of the full once-punctured-torus loop-outer group has multiplier globally one. Every finite two-subgroup consequently has multiplier values in the global units $\{1,-1\}$, determined by its dyadic coordinate. No geometric realization or conjugacy assertion is included.
depends_on: C.20–C.21; KZ 2007 Corollary 2 and Theorem 2; actual cusp filling
notes: Full versus pro-p comparison maps retained.

statement: The complete finite-multiplier consequence of LM4 D.42 Every involution of the full three-cusp loop-outer group allowing cusp permutations has multiplier equal to its global dyadic sign. Together with C.16 this proves that every finite subgroup has multiplier image in $\{1,-1\}$, determined by its dyadic coordinate. This independently supplies the transposition inputs LM4 D.36 and D.41.
depends_on: R1; C.15–C.17; exact cyclic cover and Frobenius-orbit comparison
notes: Full versus pro-p comparison maps retained.

statement: The proposed cubic lattice admits an invariant unimodular surface form Let $q\equiv1\pmod3$ be an odd prime. The $\mathbb Z_3[C_3]$-module \[ L_q=\mathbb Z_3[\zeta_3]\oplus \mathbb Z_3[C_3]^{\,q-1} \tag{C.24.1} \] admits a $C_3$-invariant unimodular alternating form. All integral fixed vectors have pairings divisible by three. This module is realized by the homology of a geometric order-three action on a closed surface of genus $(3q-1)/2$. Thus a contradiction based solely on the module (C.24.1), its surface form and mod-three isotropy of integral fixed characters cannot exclude a scalar cubic torus coordinate. This is an algebraic limitation of that approach, not a realization of such a torus coordinate.
depends_on: explicit integral matrices and equivariant handle construction
notes: No existence of a scalar cubic torus action is asserted; only linear data and a filled-surface realization.

statement: A free-factor route would settle the actual fixed kernel In the notation of C.12, if the actual other fixed group $B$ is a free profinite factor of $F=\widehat F_2$, then $B\cong\widehat{\mathbb Z}$ and $K=\ker(\chi|_B)=1$. The abstract projective retract constructed in C.2 is not a free profinite factor of $\widehat F_2$.
depends_on: C.1; C.2; C.12; full free-product Hom count
notes: The actual fixed group has not been proved to be a free profinite factor.

statement: The scalar cubic existence question in prompt C.3 We have not constructed or excluded an order-three element of the full torus loop-outer group whose multiplier has a nonidentity cubic coordinate. C.16 is specific to the three-cusp structure and does not prove the torus assertion. C.24 explains exactly why replacing the quartic involution in C.22 by the proposed cubic integral module does not yield the same contradiction: the fixed vectors come from norms in regular modules and their pairings vanish modulo three. The module is even geometrically realizable on the filled covering surface, while the needed descent to the original punctured torus with its specified nontrivial multiplier is absent. An additional cyclic-cover attempt has the following precise limit. At a scalar cubic coordinate $q$, an eigencharacter $F\to C_q$ is preserved up to a primitive cube-root scalar, rather than pointwise. The induced order-three action consequently permutes nontrivial deck eigenspaces in orbits of length three. Its commutant is no longer the product of unramified fields with multiplicity one used in C.16; the resulting permutation blocks themselves have order three. Thus absence of a nontrivial cubic root in an unramified triadic field does not exclude this different semilinear action. The finite Frobenius quotients proposed in LM4 D.71 and D.73 would impose stronger full-group constraints; without a separate proof that those constraints are incompatible, or a construction of a compatible full action, they do not answer this row.
depends_on: C.16; C.24; exact semilinear deck distinction
notes: Full versus pro-p comparison maps retained.

statement: Mixed-sign diagonal power involutions fail the full torus cusp test For $u\in\widehat{\mathbb Z}^{\times}$ with $u^2=1$, the continuous automorphism \[ \alpha_u:\widehat F(x,y)\longrightarrow\widehat F(x,y), \qquad x\longmapsto x^u,\quad y\longmapsto y^{-u} \tag{C.27.1} \] has order two and determinant $-1$ on full abelianization. It preserves the torus cusp $[x,y]$ up to conjugacy and the power $-1$ if and only if $u=1$ or $u=-1$ globally. In these two cases it is a standard reflection and its noncusp fixed group is $\widehat{\mathbb Z}$. Every pro-$p$ image of (C.27.1) is a standard reflection, including when the full cusp assertion fails. Thus this family gives an explicit mixed-prime obstruction to one natural attempted construction in prompt C.2. It does not classify general negative torus involutions.
depends_on: Finite Frobenius quotients; explicit SL2(F7) quotient; HR1985 TheoremB′
notes: For αu:x↦x^u,y↦y^(−u), u²=1, full cusp preservation is equivalent to global u=±1; all pro-p images preserve it. The surviving cases have K′=1. General negative torus conjugacy remains Open.

statement: Self-centralizing sections for every pure negative sphere action Let $n\geq2$, and let \[ F_n=\widehat{\pi_1(S_{0,n+1})} =\widehat F(x_1,\ldots,x_n),\qquad x_{n+1}=(x_1\cdots x_n)^{-1}. \] Suppose an outer involution preserves each of the $n+1$ peripheral conjugacy classes and sends each $x_j$ to a conjugate of $x_j^{-1}$. In its centre-free extension $1\to F_n\to E\to C_2\to1$, there are exactly $n+1$ $F_n$-conjugacy classes of sections. Every section $S$ satisfies \[ C_{F_n}(S)=1. \tag{C.28.1} \] In particular every genuine involutory representative has trivial fixed subgroup. The assertion concerns the full profinite group, not only its pro-$2$ quotient. More generally, let an involution act compatibly on the full profinite pure mapping class groups of the punctured spheres in a forgetful tower, preserving the individual peripheral classes of each point-pushing kernel with exponent $-1$. Its fixed subgroup in every group of this tower is trivial. The same holds in the pure braid tower, provided the two-strand group is inverted. In particular, the actual action of any multiplier-$-1$ involution of $\widehat{GT}$ on a pure braid group has trivial fixed subgroup.
depends_on: C.5–C.7; Kochloukova–Zalesskii2007 Theorem2; full profinite Birman exactness; BHR2019 §§7,11; split Fadell–Neuwirth completion argument
notes: Boolean localized cohomology gives n+1 section classes; unique-dependence cusp graph gives two endpoints each; finite-coefficient duality kills full centralizers. Compatible pure genus-zero forgetful towers have trivial fixed subgroup. No GT0 action on five points or full free-product splitting presumed. Pure braid variant includes the inverted Zhat base and all infinity cusp classes; applies to a

statement: A full boundary test for automorphisms Let $S$ be a connected compact oriented surface with $m\geq1$ boundary components and negative Euler characteristic. Let $F=\widehat{\pi_1(S)}$ be its full profinite fundamental group and let $c_1,\ldots,c_m$ be its positively oriented boundary generators, based by chosen arcs. Suppose a continuous endomorphism $\varphi:F\to F$ satisfies \[ \varphi(c_j)=g_jc_{\sigma(j)}^{\mu_j}g_j^{-1} \quad(1\leq j\leq m), \qquad \sigma\in\mathfrak S_m,\quad \mu_j\in\widehat{\mathbb Z}^{\times},\quad g_j\in F. \] Then $\varphi$ is an automorphism. If $m\geq2$, its exponents $\mu_j$ are necessarily equal. In particular, for the full profinite pants group, a substitution \[ x\longmapsto x^\mu,\qquad y\longmapsto u^{-1}y^\mu u \] with $\mu\in\widehat{\mathbb Z}^{\times}$ is an automorphism as soon as $x^\mu u^{-1}y^\mu u$ is conjugate to $(xy)^\mu$. No separate full-generation hypothesis is needed.
depends_on: Finite covering spaces; explicit boundary homology relation; full finite-index topology; profinite Hopficity
notes: Any continuous endomorphism permuting all individual boundary classes by full unit powers is automatically onto and injective; no separate generation condition. Exponents agree for at least2 boundaries. Single-boundary case explicitly included. Pants case was already asserted in LM4 D35; this is an independent covering proof, not a new existence result.

statement: Unit hexagon solutions are full automorphisms Let $F=\widehat F(x,y)$, put $z=(xy)^{-1}$, and let $\lambda\in\widehat{\mathbb Z}^{\times}$ and $f\in F'$. Write $m=(\lambda-1)/2\in\widehat{\mathbb Z}$. Suppose the following are identities in the full profinite group: \[ \begin{split} f(x,y)f(y,x)&=1,\\ f(x,y)x^m f(z,x)z^m f(y,z)y^m&=1. \end{split} \tag{C.30.1} \] Then the continuous endomorphism \[ \varphi(x)=x^\lambda,\qquad \varphi(y)=f^{-1}y^\lambda f \] is an automorphism. In particular no separate invertibility hypothesis is needed for a unit pair satisfying these two full equations. If it also satisfies the full pentagon, it belongs to the full Grothendieck--Teichm\"uller group, including its unit requirement.
depends_on: C.29; full two-equation identities; BHR2019 operadic monoid presentation
notes: Explicit third-cusp conjugator x^m f(z,x), derived without invertibility. Does not prove full pentagon implies hexagon or a unit parameter. No priority claim.

statement: Every full braid-operad endomorphism has a unit multiplier Let $\Phi$ be an object-fixing continuous endomorphism of the symmetric operad $\widehat{\mathrm{PaB}}$ of full profinite parenthesized braids. Let $\lambda\in1+2\widehat{\mathbb Z}$ be its exponent on the elementary two-strand braiding. Then \[ \lambda\in\widehat{\mathbb Z}^{\times}. \] Consequently the full Grothendieck--Teichm\"uller endomorphism monoid, defined by the full duality, hexagon and pentagon equations with an odd parameter, is already its group of units.
depends_on: BHR2019 Propositions7.3,7.7,8.1 and Definition6.4; Horel2017; Marin2012; full braid goodness and finite cohomological dimension; C.30
notes: Exact ribbon cabling gives phi(z_n)=z_n^lambda without surjectivity; arity-p central-root construction would create p-torsion if p divides lambda. Does not make a bare pentagon satisfy hexagons.

statement: The relative pro-$p$ braid monoid has unit parameter Fix a prime $p$. Suppose that $\mu\in1+2\mathbb Z_p$ and $f\in(F_2^{(p)})'$ satisfy the duality, hexagon and pentagon equations in the corresponding pro-$p$ pure groups. Then $\mu\in\mathbb Z_p^\times$. In particular the pro-$p$ Grothendieck--Teichm\"uller endomorphism monoid is its unit group.
depends_on: C.31 braid/ribbon presentation; Cohen2010 almost-direct decomposition; explicit full induced pro-p topology and p-goodness
notes: The relative completion retains S_n; its Sylow-p preimages are completions of discrete finite-index groups with finite cd_p. Excludes every integral p-divisible parameter including0.

statement: An integral pro-$p$ pentagon has a square-unit parameter Let $f\in F_2^{(p)}$ satisfy the pentagon in $P_4^{(p)}$, and use the convention $[x,y]=xyx^{-1}y^{-1}$ for its coefficient $c_2(f)$. Then \[ D=1+24c_2(f)\in(\mathbb Z_p^\times)^2. \tag{C.33.1} \] For either root $\mu\in\mathbb Z_p^\times$, the pair $(\mu,f)$ satisfies the actual pro-$p$ hexagons and belongs to the pro-$p$ Grothendieck--Teichm\"uller group. In particular the canonical full pentagon word in A.37 has a peripheral conjugator with that prescribed word at every maximal pro-$p$ quotient.
depends_on: Furusho2010 Theorem2/Corollary12; integral Magnus module; exact affine hexagon; coefficient of degree p-1; C.32
notes: For nonzero D the integral series R forces D^((p-1)/2)=1 modp; C.32 separately excludesD0. All maximal pro-p conjugators exist with prescribed canonical word. Does not prove full profinite hexagon or marked conjugacy.

statement: A specified full square root need not satisfy the hexagon The literal prescribed-root assertion in Furusho's Question 14 \cite{Furusho2010} is false: a full profinite pentagon word $f$ and a specified unit $\mu$ satisfying $\mu^2=1+24c_2(f)$ need not satisfy the full hexagon. This does not refute the existential assertion that some choice of such a root satisfies it.
depends_on: A.39 mixed-sign S4 example; direct hexagon evaluation
notes: f=1 and mu_2=-1,mu_odd=1 gives mu7mod24,m3mod12; x=(234),y=(1234) gives hexagon x!=1. Existential root assertion remains open in general and works here with ±1.

statement: The canonical word has full duality and passes every tetrahedral generation test Let \(\alpha=(-1,f)\in\widehat{GT}_0\) be a nonidentity involution, and let \(u\in F'\) be its unique R1 parameter, \(u=f\alpha(u)\). Then \[ u(y,x)=u(x,y)^{-1}. \tag{C.35.1} \] For every continuous epimorphism \(q:F\twoheadrightarrow A_4\), \[ \big\langle q(x),q(u)^{-1}q(y)q(u)\big\rangle=A_4. \tag{C.35.2} \] Thus the full canonical substitution passes every \(A_4\) generation test. No pentagon hypothesis is needed for this assertion, and no full generation or third-cusp assertion is inferred from it.
depends_on: R1 full uniqueness; GT0 two-cycle and negative hexagon
notes: No pentagon hypothesis is used. No full generation or third-cusp conclusion is claimed. Binary tetrahedral matrices eliminate both (3,3,2) and (3,3,3) collapse passports.

statement: Tetrahedral third-cusp tests and dyadic generation over the full modulo-three base Retain the hypotheses and canonical word \(u\) of C.35. For every \(\mu\in\widehat{\mathbb Z}^{\times}\) and every continuous homomorphism \(q:F\to A_4\), one has \[ q\bigl(x^\mu u^{-1}y^\mu u\bigr) \sim_{A_4}q\bigl((xy)^\mu\bigr). \tag{C.36.1} \] Put \[ U_3=\ker\bigl(F\to C_3^2\bigr)=\overline{F'F^3},\qquad G_{3,2}=F/O^2(U_3). \tag{C.36.2} \] For every such \(\mu\), the normalized substitution \[ x\longmapsto x^\mu,\qquad y\longmapsto u^{-1}y^\mu u \tag{C.36.3} \] induces an automorphism of the actual relative pro-two group \(G_{3,2}\), and intertwines the induced actions of the given \(\alpha\) and standard \(c\). In particular this proves the canonical generation condition at the specified \(U=F'F^3\) relative level. The full relative third-cusp condition is not asserted.
depends_on: C.35; R1 identity; rank-ten Cayley-graph Frattini module over F2[C3²]
notes: Actual relative pro-two quotient, not maximal pro-two. The argument does not prove its relative third-cusp equation or full generation.

statement: The canonical word passes every icosahedral generation test Let \(\alpha=(-1,f)\) be an involution of the full \(\widehat{\mathrm{GT}}_0\), and let \(u\in F'\) be its unique full R1 word, so that \(u=f\alpha(u)\). Then, for every continuous epimorphism \(q:F\to A_5\) and every \(\mu\in\widehat{\mathbb Z}^{\times}\), \[ \bigl\langle q(x^\mu),q(u^{-1}y^\mu u)\bigr\rangle=A_5. \tag{C.37.1} \] This is an assertion about each individual finite quotient. It does not assert generation in the joint quotient consisting of all nineteen \(A_5\) factors, a relative pro-\(p\) completion, or the full group \(F\); nor does it identify the third cusp. No pentagon equation is used.
notes: Exact SL2(F5) and independent S5 certificates. No pentagon. Joint A5 head generation and third-cusp conjugacy are not asserted.

statement: The paired involution has exactly the peripheral coinvariant kernel Retain \(\alpha,u,v\), and \(\tau=\alpha v\) from C.37, and put \(z=(xy)^{-1}\). Let \[ N_\tau=\overline{\langle\!\langle \tau(g)g^{-1}:g\in F\rangle\!\rangle}_F, \qquad N_z=\overline{\langle\!\langle z\rangle\!\rangle}_F . \] Then \[ N_\tau=N_z,\qquad F/N_\tau\simeq\widehat{\mathbb Z}. \tag{C.38.1} \] Moreover there are a local involutory section \(r\in F\rtimes_\tau C_2\) that inverts \(z\), and \(g\in F\), such that \[ z=[g,r]. \tag{C.38.2} \] Equivalently \(z\) is \(F\)-conjugate to a single twisted commutator \(h\tau(h)^{-1}\). These equalities do not assert that \(g,r\) generate the semidirect product, or identify that group with a free profinite product.
notes: The quotient is Zhat. No free-product recognition or generation by the selected section and conjugator is asserted.

statement: Every peripheral involution passes the symmetric-four test and the dyadic relative \(S_3\) levels Let \(\alpha=(-1,f)\) be an involution in the full peripheral group \(\mathcal P\), with its normalized representative and full R1 word \(u\in F'\), so that \(u=f\alpha(u)\). For every epimorphism \(q:F\to S_4\) and every \(\mu\in\widehat{\mathbb Z}^{\times}\), \[ \bigl\langle q(x^\mu),q(u^{-1}y^\mu u)\bigr\rangle=S_4. \tag{C.39.1} \] For every epimorphism \(q_3:F\to S_3\), put \(U=\ker q_3\). The normalized substitution \[ \theta_\mu:x\longmapsto x^\mu,\qquad y\longmapsto u^{-1}y^\mu u \] induces an automorphism of the actual relative pro-two group \[ F/O^2(U), \tag{C.39.2} \] and intertwines the induced \(\alpha\) and \(c\). Neither duality nor a hexagon or pentagon is assumed. These are generation and unmarked conjugacy statements; relative third-cusp preservation is not asserted.
depends_on: full R1;C.28;A.44 reflection case;finite two-group Frattini
notes: No duality/hexagon/pentagon assumption. Exact nine-orbit certificate. The finite quotient need not inherit an endomorphism. Relative third cusp is not asserted.

statement: The correctly normalized third cusp holds in every symmetric-four quotient Let \(\alpha=(-1,f)\) be an involution of the full \(\widehat{\mathrm{GT}}_0\), and let \(u\in F'\) be its canonical full R1 word. In the universal full dihedral quotient \[ D=\widehat{\mathbb Z}(t)\rtimes\langle a\rangle,\qquad a^2=1,\quad ata=t^{-1},\qquad x\longmapsto a,\quad y\longmapsto at, \] write \(u\longmapsto t^\kappa\), and set \[ d=2\kappa+1. \tag{C.40.1} \] By A.45, \(d\) is a full unit. Since \(D'=\overline{\langle t^2\rangle}\) and \(u\in F'\), one has \(\kappa\in2\widehat{\mathbb Z}\) and \(d\equiv1\pmod4\). This is the global-sign normalization of the possible multipliers \(\{d,-d\}\). For every continuous homomorphism \(q:F\to S_4\), \[ q\bigl(x^d u^{-1}y^d u\bigr)\sim_{S_4}q\bigl((xy)^d\bigr). \tag{C.40.2} \] Moreover, if \(J_4\) is the intersection of all epimorphism kernels \(F\to S_4\), both the normalized substitution \(\theta_d=(d,u)\) and \(\psi=(1,u)\) induce automorphisms of the actual joint finite quotient \(F/J_4\). The result asserts no full or relative third-cusp identity.
notes: d=2kappa+1 is the global sign with d=1 mod4. Six common S3 head cases, all binary necessary tables checked. No finite realization assumption, no full/relative third-cusp assertion.

statement: An explicit first relation-module bound for the canonical word Let $F=\widehat F(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$, let $c(x_i)=x_i^{-1}$, and let $q:F\to Q$ be a finite quotient with $c$-stable kernel $U$. Put $\Phi_2(U)=\overline{U^2[U,U]}$. Then \[ C_{F/\Phi_2(U)}(c)\longrightarrow F/U \quad\hbox{has trivial image}. \tag{C.41.1} \] For the rank-two canonical equation $u=f\alpha(u)$, where $\alpha(x)=x^{-1}$ and $\alpha(y)=f^{-1}y^{-1}f$, this gives the explicit implication \[ f\in\Phi_2(U)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad u\in U. \tag{C.41.2} \] The latter assertion concerns the actual full canonical word and a $c$-stable $U$. It does not say that the fixed subgroup inside the relation module itself is trivial.
notes: Reconstructed after environment loss from accepted proof. The A5 exclusion is conditional on f vanishing in the enlarged quotient; fixed kernel cycles can remain.

statement: One dyadic homology step determines the canonical head Let $F$ be a finitely generated free profinite group, let $\sigma$ be an involution, and suppose every involution of $E=F\rtimes_\sigma C_2$ has centralizer exactly its order-two subgroup. If $U\trianglelefteq F$ is open and $\sigma$-stable, then \[ C_{F/\Phi_2(U)}(\sigma)\longrightarrow F/U \quad\hbox{has trivial image}. \tag{C.42.1} \] More precisely, two actual sections of $U\rtimes_\sigma C_2$ that are conjugate modulo $\Phi_2(U)$ are already $U$-conjugate. The hypotheses hold for every pure negative sphere action in C.28, in particular for every full negative pants involution. For the actual rank-two canonical equation $u=f\alpha(u)$, all solutions of its induced equation in $F/\Phi_2(U)$ have the same image in $F/U$, namely the image of the unique full word $u$. Thus that head value is determined by finite data at this explicit relative level. This does not compute an unspecified existential parameter $f$, prove generation, or settle the third cusp.
notes: Reconstructed after environment loss from accepted proof. No generation, third-cusp or free-product recognition assertion.

statement: Self-centralizing sections for the regular pants involution Let $F=\widehat F(x,y)$ and $z=(xy)^{-1}$. Suppose an involution $\sigma$ interchanges the peripheral classes of $x$ and $y$ with exponent $-1$, and preserves the class of $z$ with exponent $-1$. Then $E=F\rtimes_\sigma C_2$ has exactly one $F$-conjugacy class of sections, and every section $S$ satisfies $C_F(S)=1$. Every open $\sigma$-stable subgroup inherits self-centralizing torsion in its split extension. In particular, if $U$ is also normal in $F$, the map $C_{F/\Phi_2(U)}(\sigma)\to F/U$ has trivial image.
depends_on: C.5;C.6 orbit relative duality;C.37 one-section count;C.42;Kochloukova-Zalesskii Theorem2
notes: The swapped pair stays in the relative module until localization. No free-product recognition or generation follows. Finite r-frame remains variable under A16; failure of one stored frame is not a full obstruction.

statement: A full unit and relative pronilpotent conjugacy for the regular pants action Let $F=\widehat F(x,y)$, put $z=(xy)^{-1}$, and use the free basis $(x,z)$. Let $\sigma$ be a regular negative pants involution as in C.43, normalized so that $\sigma(z)=z^{-1}$ literally. Put $K=\langle\!\langle z\rangle\!\rangle_F$ and $A=F/K=\widehat{\mathbb Z}$, with generator the image of $x$. There is a unique $g\in F$ such that \[ \sigma(g)g^{-1}=z. \tag{C.44.1} \] Its image $a\in A$ belongs to $\widehat{\mathbb Z}^{\times}$. Moreover, the substitution $\varphi(x)=g$, $\varphi(z)=z$ induces an automorphism of \[ G=F/R_{\mathrm{nil}}(K),\qquad R_{\mathrm{nil}}(K)=\bigcap_p O^p(K), \tag{C.44.2} \] where $O^p(K)$ is the residual for finite $p$-group quotients, and conjugates the standard regular action $\rho(x)=zx$, $\rho(z)=z^{-1}$ to $\sigma$ on $G$. The conjugacy asserted here is in $\operatorname{Aut}(G)$. No preservation of the original three peripheral classes by $\varphi$, or generation of the full group $F$ by $g,z$, is asserted.
depends_on: C.43; exact cyclic-cover Alexander module; compact group-ring division; all-prime Frattini; distinct-prime product comparison
notes: Conjugacy in Aut(F/R_nil(<<z>>)) and every Aut(F/O^p(<<z>>)); no original peripheral marking or full F generation assertion. All odd-prime characters force the full unit.

statement: The invariant metric and compact-core collapse The function \[ d_Q(u,v)=\sup_{q\in Q}d(qu,qv) \] is a bounded $Q$-invariant metric inducing the original topology on $O$. If $A,B\subset O$ are compact, $a_j\in A$, and $q_ja_j\to z\in\partial\overline D$, then $q_jB\to\{z\}$ uniformly in the original metric.

The exact $C_0$ image and compact-parameter criterion For $h\in C_{\operatorname{Homeo}(O)}(Q)$ define \[ \delta_h(\pi u)=d_Q(hu,u),\qquad V=\{h\in C_{\operatorname{Homeo}(O)}(Q):\delta_h\in C_0(N)\}. \] Here $C_0(N)$ consists of continuous functions vanishing uniformly outside compact subsets. Restriction $C\to V$ and extension by the identity on $\partial\overline D$ are inverse isometric topological group isomorphisms, for the sums of the uniform distances of maps and inverses. For a compact metrizable parameter space $P$, an equivariant family $h_s$ with continuous evaluation $P\times O\to O$ extends jointly to the closed disk if and only if \begin{equation}\label{eq:DE-tail} \forall\epsilon>0\ \exists K\Subset N:\quad \sup_{s\in P,\,\pi u\notin K}d_Q(h_su,u)<\epsilon. \end{equation} Joint continuity of the extended inverse family follows as well. This proves LM4 C.88 with its stated hypotheses.

Pointed descent, its image, and its stronger topology Let \[ I_p=\operatorname{Homeo}(N\mathbin{\mathrm{rel}}p)_0 \] denote the identity path component in the compact-open topology on maps and inverses. Every $a\in F$ descends to $I_p$. Every $b\in I_p$ has a unique lift $\lambda(b):O\to O$ fixing $x$, and that lift commutes with every element of $Q$. Define \[ B_p=\{b\in I_p:\delta_{\lambda(b)}\in C_0(N)\}. \] Descent gives a group isomorphism $F\to B_p$ and an isometry if $B_p$ is given the metric \begin{align*} d^{\uparrow}(b,c)={}&\sup_{u\in O}d_Q(\lambda(b)u,\lambda(c)u)\\ &+\sup_{u\in O}d_Q(\lambda(b)^{-1}u,\lambda(c)^{-1}u). \end{align*} For compact parameter spaces, continuity in this metric is exactly compact-open continuity downstairs together with \eqref{eq:DE-tail} for the actual pointed lifts. This proves LM4 C.92, including its distinction between the two topologies.

Evaluation has a global section in the original topology For every quotient $N$ under consideration, compact or noncompact, there is a continuous map $s:O\to C$ with $s(y)x=y$ and $s(x)=1$. Consequently \[ C\xrightarrow{\ \cong\ }O\times F,\qquad a\longmapsto\bigl(ax,s(ax)^{-1}a\bigr) \] is a homeomorphism, with inverse $(y,f)\mapsto s(y)f$. In particular $\pi_j(F,1)\to\pi_j(C,1)$ is an isomorphism for all $j\geq1$.

The compact quotient case is contractible If $N$ is compact, $C$ admits a continuous contraction to $1$ fixing $1$ throughout. This proves both LM4 C.90 and LM4 C.91, including the torus and Klein-bottle quotients.

Compact-open convergence does not control the lifted tail There are operators satisfying all the hypotheses above, with $N=S^1\times\mathbb R$, and $b_R\in B_p$ converging to $1$ in $I_p$ while $d^{\uparrow}(b_R,1)>2/5$ for every $R\geq2$.

Families with one compact quotient support fill Let $a:S^m\to C$ be a based sphere family, $m\geq1$, and suppose that one compact set $K\Subset N$ satisfies $a_\xi(u)=u$ whenever $\pi u\notin K$. Then $a$ has a based null-homotopy in $C$ with one compact quotient support, and hence with a uniform tail.

The trivial operator case and the compact-open exception If $Q=1$, the whole group $C$ and every point stabilizer $F$ are contractible in their actual topology, even though the identity component of $\operatorname{Homeo}(\mathbb R^2\mathbin{\mathrm{rel}}0)$ in the interior compact-open topology has homotopy type $S^1$.

The arbitrary noncompact quotient uniform-tail deformation Assume the quotient $N$ is noncompact. Let $P$ be a compact metrizable space and $a:P\to F$ a continuous map. Does $a$ admit a homotopy to the constant identity that is continuous in the metric $d^{\uparrow}$? The relative version for a prescribed subset on which $a=1$ is also undecided here. In particular we have not proved or refuted $\pi_1(C,1)=0$ in this generality. The precise missing estimate is \eqref{eq:DE-tail} uniformly in $(s,t)\in P\times[0,1]$. The unqualified compact-open contraction of a pointed noncompact surface does not supply it, as D.6 makes concrete. A sufficient constructive route is a deformation of every based sphere family to one with common compact quotient support, preserving this estimate; D.7 would then finish the sphere. No such cutoff has been constructed for an arbitrary $d_Q$. We checked the later uniform-deformation literature as well. Yagasaki's covering-space theorem has a compact base \cite[Theorem 1.1]{DE_Yagasaki2014}. Its end theorem assumes specified Euclidean ends. The later end theorem requires finitely many isolated proper product ends with the stated end-deformation property \cite[Theorem 1.3]{DE_Yagasaki2018}. Neither hypothesis follows from the present data. In particular the bounded metric $d_Q$ need not be a proper end metric, and no comparison transferring the needed deformation to $d^{\uparrow}$ has been proved. We also considered equivariant deformations of a null lifted triangulation. Its pointwise skeleton stabilizer contracts. The family of skeleton embeddings still requires a deformation with the same uniform control. The escaping sequence in D.6 has not been turned into a nontrivial loop; presenting it as one would be an error.
notes: Open: no uniform-tail contraction or nontrivial loop obtained; compact-open contraction does not suffice.

statement: Arbitrary-frontier descent in the exact comparison Let $U$ be a simply connected open orbit in the original surface. The prime-end disk need not map continuously onto its closure. When the interior identification has such an extension, its boundary map may fail to be injective. We have not proved that an intrinsic centralizer filling can be chosen to extend over every such original frontier, with jointly continuous inverses. An interior conjugacy alone does not suffice. One must retain all original approach limits and prescribed frontier values; a boundary equivalence relation describes only the cases where a continuous boundary map exists. This is the arbitrary-frontier descent obligation listed in LM4 C.12.
notes: Open: original approach limits and jointly continuous inverses must be preserved; a continuous prime-end boundary quotient need not exist.

statement: Nonfixed-frontier pasting and infinitely many orbit types The remaining LM4 C.12 comparison requires simultaneous fillings on all open orbits agreeing with a deforming, possibly nonfixed, nonopen locus, including infinitely many operator-inequivalent remaining components and accumulation outside the treated closed sets. We have not proved or refuted this assertion. The missing conditions are (i) existence of mutually compatible restrictions on every common frontier, (ii) extension of these restrictions over the incident open orbits, and (iii) uniform control of both maps and inverses across arbitrary accumulating families. D.2 controls one original disk with fixed boundary and does not supply these three comparisons.
notes: Open: frontier agreement and uniform inverse control under arbitrary accumulation remain.

statement: The universal admissible level-zero kernel For an admissible punctured surface, with actual homeomorphism group $A$, a strict action $u:\Gamma\to A$, and $H=u(\Gamma)$, the unresolved comparison of LM4 C.12 is injectivity of \[ \pi_1(C_A(H),1)\longrightarrow\pi_1(A,1)^\Gamma. \] For hyperbolic finite-type surfaces the target is zero, so the question is whether every based centralizer loop contracts in the centralizer. For the plane, annulus, and torus the respective targets are the invariant subgroups of $\mathbb Z$, $\mathbb Z$, and $\mathbb Z^2$. No counterexample inside this admitted category and no proof covering D.9--D.11 is obtained here. The unpunctured sphere example mentioned in LM4 C.12 is outside the stated category and cannot settle this assertion.
notes: Open: excluded unpunctured sphere does not decide the admissible comparison.

statement: Planar filling hulls preserve the invariant diameter bound Choose closed-disk coordinates in which $d$ is Euclidean, and retain $d_Q(u,v)=\sup_q|qu-qv|$. This changes neither the actual group topology nor its $C_0$ tail condition. For a nonempty compact $A\subset O$, let $\operatorname{Fill}(A)$ be $A$ together with all relatively compact components of $O\setminus A$. Then \[ q\operatorname{Fill}(A)=\operatorname{Fill}(qA),\qquad \operatorname{diam}_{d_Q}\operatorname{Fill}(A) =\operatorname{diam}_{d_Q}(A). \] Moreover, if $A\subset B_{d_Q}(x,r)$ is compact, then $\operatorname{Fill}(A)\subset B_{d_Q}(x,r)$. Every connected component of a $d_Q$-ball is a simply connected open planar domain. In particular every loop contained in one such ball has a filling in that same ball.
notes: Ball components simply connected; does not supply controlled parametric ambient isotopy.

statement: An inner-diameter metric retaining every based sphere family Inner-diameter metrics also occur in \cite[Definition 2.2]{DE_Fabel1998}. With the invariant metric in D.13, put \[ \rho(u,v)=\inf\{\operatorname{diam}_{d_Q}(\alpha): \alpha\subset O\text{ is an arc joining }u\text{ to }v\}. \] Then $\rho$ is a bounded $Q$-invariant metric inducing the original interior topology, and $d_Q\leq\rho$. Its open balls are path connected. If $U(u,r)$ is the component of $B_{d_Q}(u,r)$ containing $u$, then $U(u,r)$ is an open topological disk and \[ B_\rho(u,r)\subset U(u,r)\subset B_\rho(u,2r). \] Every map $S^j\to B_\rho(u,r)$, $j\geq1$, is null-homotopic in $B_\rho(u,2r)$. Let $F^\rho\subset F$ consist of maps whose lift displacement for $\rho$ belongs to $C_0(N)$, equipped with the uniform $\rho$ topology on maps and inverses. Every based continuous family $P\to F$ from a compact, connected, locally path-connected metric space is also a continuous family into $F^\rho$, with a uniform $\rho$ tail. Consequently inclusion $F^\rho\to F$ induces isomorphisms on every positive based homotopy group. This reduces the sphere-family part of D.9 to a metric with connected balls and the displayed uniform filling bound; it does not prove the ambient deformation.
notes: Bρ(u,r) lies in an open disk U(u,r) inside Bρ(u,2r); positive based homotopy groups are preserved. Controlled equivariant ambient isotopy remains unproved.

statement: Arbitrary simply connected frontiers with trivial operators Let $U\subset S^2$ be a simply connected open domain whose complement $K$ contains at least two points. Give \[ H_U=\{h\in\operatorname{Homeo}^+(S^2):h|_K=1_K\} \] the original uniform topology on maps and inverses. Then $H_U$ is homeomorphic to the separable Hilbert space $\ell^2$ and has an identity-fixed contraction. In particular every compact family in this group contracts with joint continuity on the original sphere, even when $\partial U$ is not locally connected. This settles the trivial-operator case of the arbitrary-frontier obligation. It does not assert an equivariant contraction for nontrivial operators.
notes: Original sphere-uniform topology; no local connectedness required; complement must be nondegenerate. No equivariant contraction asserted.

statement: An obstruction to global equivariant compression Suppose a continuous $Q$-equivariant map $e:O\to O$ has image contained in $\pi^{-1}(S)$ for some compact connected subsurface $S\subset N$. Then $Q$ is finitely generated. In particular, when $Q$ is infinitely generated, there is no $Q$-equivariant embedding that compresses all of $O$ over one compact quotient core. This rules out that direct adaptation of the compression step of D.15; it does not refute D.9.
depends_on: Covering endpoint identification;finite generation of compact-surface groups
notes: Only a method obstruction: a Q-equivariant map into the preimage of a compact quotient core forces Q finitely generated. Does not refute the group contraction.

statement: Joint equivariant map fillings with a uniform quotient tail Let $P$ be a compact connected locally path-connected metric space, and let $a:P\to F$ be continuous and based at the identity. Put $A=\{s\in P:a_s=1\}$. There is a jointly continuous map \[ E:P\times[0,1]\times\overline D\longrightarrow\overline D \] such that $E_{s,0}=a_s$, $E_{s,1}=1$, and $E_{s,t}=1$ for $s\in A$. Every $E_{s,t}$ fixes the original boundary and $x$, maps $O$ into $O$, and commutes there with $Q$. Moreover there is a positive function $\eta\in C_0(N)$ such that \[ \rho(E_{s,t}(v),v)\leq128\eta(\pi v) \quad(s\in P, t\in[0,1], v\in O). \] Thus the construction retains the uniform quotient tail and joint continuity in the evaluated point. The construction does not preserve injectivity. In particular this statement does not give a filling in $F$.
notes: Explicit displacement bound 128 eta; triangulated quotient and Tietze extension inside controlled open-disk carriers. Injectivity of intermediate maps is not proved; D.9 remains Open.

statement: The compact real-type injection of LM6 C.13 For $g\geq2$, the topological types of orientation-reversing involutions of $S_g$ inject into conjugacy classes in $\operatorname{Out}(\widehat{\pi_1(S_g)})$. They consequently inject into conjugacy classes in $Q_g^{\pm}$ and $P_g^{\pm}$. For genus three the six types are \[ (r,a)=(0,1),(1,1),(2,1),(3,1),(2,0),(4,0). \tag{E.1.1} \]
depends_on: BZ 2025 Theorem A at p=2; surface goodness; oval homology
notes: Full profinite groups unless explicitly designated pro-p or procongruence.

statement: Marked incidence and the simultaneous orientation in LM6 C.14 The injection of E.1 holds for individually labelled real markings, and for unordered markings allowing nonreal conjugate pairs. A peripheral isomorphism of the completed real surface extensions recovers the cyclic incidence of real marked points on each oval. For dividing surfaces, the cyclic orders on labelled marked ovals are identified only by their simultaneous reversal.
depends_on: E.1; full peripheral maps; finite graph covers
notes: Full profinite groups unless explicitly designated pro-p or procongruence.

statement: The exact nonabelian-cohomology fibre of LM6 C.15 Let $1\to K\to P^{\pm}\xrightarrow{q}Q^{\pm}\to1$ be a continuous exact sequence of profinite groups with compatible orientation characters, with $K\leq P$ their positive kernel. Fix an orientation-reversing involution $\tau\in P^{\pm}$ and put $\alpha=\operatorname{Ad}(\tau)$ and $\bar\tau=q(\tau)$. For $k\in K$ satisfying $k\alpha(k)=1$, identify cocycles by $k\sim b k\alpha(b)^{-1}$, $b\in K$. Then \begin{align} q(g)\star[k]&=[gk\alpha(g)^{-1}],\notag\\ \{\text{$P$-classes over }[\bar\tau]\} &\cong C_Q(\bar\tau)\backslash H^1(C_2,K), \tag{E.3.1}\\ 1\longrightarrow K^{k\tau}\longrightarrow C_P(k\tau) &\xrightarrow{q} \operatorname{Stab}_{C_Q(\bar\tau)}([k]) \longrightarrow1 . \tag{E.3.2} \end{align} Here $g\in P$ is any lift of the indicated quotient-centralizer element. The action need not fix the class of the trivial cocycle.
notes: Quotient-centralizer action may move the trivial cocycle class; D8 example checked.

statement: The hyperelliptic comparison of LM6 C.16 uses only the element theorem Fix a hyperelliptic involution $\iota\in\Gamma_3$, and put $H^{\pm}=C_{\Gamma_3^{\pm}}(\iota)$ and $H=H^{\pm}\cap\Gamma_3$. The natural map $\widehat{H^{\pm}}\to P_3^{\pm}$ is injective, with image $\overline{H^{\pm}}$. Each orientation-reversing involution in this image is $\overline H$-conjugate to a discrete one. For such a discrete involution $\tau$, \[ C_{P_3}(\tau)\cap\overline H =\overline{C_H(\tau)}. \tag{E.4.1} \] Each of the six types in (E.1.1) has a representative in $H^{\pm}$. No centralizer equality for a nonsolvable finite subgroup is used in these assertions.
depends_on: Boggi 2024 Theorem 7.1; BZ 2025 Theorem A at p=2
notes: Full profinite groups unless explicitly designated pro-p or procongruence.

statement: The five oval centralizers of LM6 C.17 Let $\tau\in\Gamma_3^{\pm}$ be a real involution with $r>0$, and put $C=C_{\Gamma_3}(\tau)$. The restriction of $q$ is an isomorphism \[ \overline C^{\,P_3}\xrightarrow{\sim} C_{Q_3}(\bar\tau)=\overline C^{\,Q_3},\qquad C_{P_3}(\tau)=K_c^\tau\rtimes\overline C^{\,P_3}. \tag{E.5.1} \] For these five types the quotient-centralizer action of E.3 fixes the trivial cohomology class. Formula (E.5.1) does not compute $K_c^\tau$.
depends_on: E.2; Boggi 2014 Theorem 4.5; Boggi 2020 genus ≤2 comparison; BZ element theorem
notes: Full profinite groups unless explicitly designated pro-p or procongruence.

statement: The free real type has the exact comparison of LM6 C.18 For the fixed-point-free genus-three involution $\tau$, put $N_4=S_3/\tau$, $E=\widehat{\pi_1(N_4)}$, and $\Pi=\widehat{\pi_1(S_3)}$. Let $\operatorname{Aut}_{Q}(E;\Pi)$ be the continuous automorphisms preserving $\Pi$ whose restrictions have outer class in $Q_3^{\pm}$. Then \[ \mathcal A:=\operatorname{Aut}_{Q}(E;\Pi)/\operatorname{Inn}(E) \cong C_{Q_3^{\pm}}(\bar\tau)/\langle\bar\tau\rangle \cong C_{Q_3}(\bar\tau). \tag{E.6.1} \] Under this homeomorphism the closure of $\operatorname{Mod}(N_4)$ equals the closure of $C_{\Gamma_3}(\tau)$ in $Q_3$. Equality of this closure with $\mathcal A$ remains a density question.
notes: Full profinite groups unless explicitly designated pro-p or procongruence.

statement: The obstruction to a hyperelliptic reduction in LM6 C.19 For the positive lift $j:\operatorname{Mod}(N_4)\cong C_{\Gamma_3}(\tau)$ and every finite-index subgroup $H\leq\operatorname{Mod}(N_4)$, the centralizer $C_{\Gamma_3}(j(H))$ has no nonidentity finite-order element. In particular $j(H)$ is never contained in a hyperelliptic centralizer, and the standard hyperelliptic subgroup of $\operatorname{Mod}(N_4)$ has infinite index.
depends_on: Farb–Margalit Propositions 2.3, 3.20 and Lemma 3.17; signed pants lifts
notes: Full profinite groups unless explicitly designated pro-p or procongruence.

statement: Finite quotients retain the entire fixed group and nonabelian cohomology Let a finite group $C_2=\langle\tau\rangle$ act continuously on a profinite group $K$, and let $N$ range over its open normal $\tau$-invariant subgroups. There are natural homeomorphisms \[ K^\tau\cong\varprojlim_N(K/N)^\tau, \qquad H^1(C_2,K)\cong\varprojlim_N H^1(C_2,K/N). \tag{E.8.1} \] The cohomology set is given the quotient topology of its compact cocycle space. Neither the maps to individual finite fixed groups nor the finite cohomology transition maps are asserted to be surjective.
notes: Full profinite groups unless explicitly designated pro-p or procongruence.

statement: The fixed congruence kernel is the fibre of oval stabilizers For one of the five oval types in E.5, let $A$ be its oval multicurve and $L=\operatorname{Stab}_{\Gamma_3}(A)$. Use E.5 to regard $\widehat L$ as a closed subgroup of $P_3$ mapping isomorphically onto $(Q_3)_A$. Then the fibre over the identity coset of the continuous map \[ P_3/\widehat L\longrightarrow Q_3/(Q_3)_A \] is naturally the profinite set $K_c$. Its $\tau$-fixed subset is naturally $K_c^\tau$.
depends_on: E.5; fibre of the multicurve-stabilizer map
notes: Full profinite groups unless explicitly designated pro-p or procongruence.

statement: The six congruence-kernel computations in prompt E.1 For each type (E.1.1), determine $K_c^\tau$ and the nonabelian pointed set $H^1(C_2,K_c)$ for $\operatorname{Ad}(\tau)$. E.3 gives the exact class and centralizer formula after these groups and sets are known; E.5 supplies its quotient-centralizer term for the five oval types. For $(0,1)$ the density question in E.6 remains an additional unresolved term. statement: The holomorphic classification of five-point configurations The possible full holomorphic automorphism groups are \[ 1,\quad C_2,\quad C_4,\quad D_3,\quad D_5. \] If the maximum order $\nu$ of a nonidentity holomorphic automorphism is $5$, $4$, or $3$, there is exactly one isomorphism class, respectively \[ \mu_5,\qquad\{\infty\}\cup\mu_4, \qquad\{0,\infty\}\cup\mu_3. \] Their full groups are $D_5,C_4,D_3$. The labeled structures are, respectively, an unoriented pentagon, a distinguished point with an oriented square on the other four points, and a three-set together with its two-element orientation torsor. These assertions verify the holomorphic classification on cote 148, scan 34, handwritten p.~1.

The one-parameter involution locus and the square and tetrahedron cases Every five-point configuration with a nontrivial holomorphic involution can be written \[ K_t=\{\infty,1,-1,t,-t\},\qquad t\ne0,\ \ t^2\ne1. \] For a configuration with the involution specified, its isomorphism class is determined by \[ \lambda=t^2,\qquad\beta=\lambda+\lambda^{-1}\in\mathbb C\setminus\{2\}. \] The full group is $C_2$ except at \[ \begin{array}{c|ccc} \beta&-2&-10/3&18\\\hline \operatorname{Aut}^+(K_t)&C_4&D_3&D_5. \end{array} \] A harmonic four-set together with a fixed point of one of its fixed-point-free involutions gives $\beta=-2$ or $34$. The second case has full group $C_2$; it is neither the pentagonal nor the square-pyramidal case. An equianharmonic four-set with such a fixed point gives $\beta=-14$ and full group $C_2$. These formulas complete the calculation begun and then crossed out on cote 148, scan 35, handwritten p.~2, and answer its question about adding an edge midpoint to a spherical square.

Every finite antiholomorphic automorphism preserving five marks has order two The inference in cote 148, scan 35, handwritten p.~2, that an even-order antiholomorphic automorphism preserving five points must fix a marked point and therefore have order two is false. The exact possible orders of antiholomorphic automorphisms of five-point configurations are $2,6,10$.

statement: Real involutions, dimensions, and their exact relation to the symmetric square An antiholomorphic \emph{involution} preserving five marked points has a fixed circle and fixes exactly $r=1,3,$ or $5$ of the marks. Each of these three spaces of real pairs $(\mathbb P^1,K,\sigma)$ has real dimension two. The examples in cote 148, scan 36, handwritten p.~3, are valid: the pentagonal configuration has an $r=5$ real structure, the triangular bipyramid has an $r=3$ structure, and the square pyramid has an $r=1$ structure. These examples are not exclusive to the indicated type.

The generic real involution locus For $K_t$ of E.31 with full positive group $C_2$, a real structure exists exactly when $\beta$ is real. The full extended group is then $C_2\times C_2$, and the fixed-mark counts of its two negative involutions are \[ \begin{array}{c|c} \text{range of }\beta&\text{counts}\\\hline \beta>2&\{5,1\}\\ \beta<-2&\{3,3\}\\ -2<\beta<2&\{1,1\}. \end{array} \] The enhanced values in E.31 are omitted from the indicated ranges.

Reflection section classes for five punctures Let $U=\mathbb P^1\setminus K$ and let $\sigma$ be a real involution fixing $r\in\{1,3,5\}$ marks. Put $m=(5-r)/2$. Its discrete orbifold extension is \[ 1\longrightarrow\pi_1(U)\longrightarrow E_\sigma\longrightarrow C_2\longrightarrow1, \qquad E_\sigma\cong\Bigl(\mathop{*}_{j=1}^{r}C_2\Bigr)*F_m. \] The sign map is nontrivial on each $C_2$ factor and trivial on $F_m$. It has exactly $r$ conjugacy classes of sections under $\pi_1(U)$, one for each component of $U^\sigma$; every section has trivial fixed subgroup in $\pi_1(U)$. This verifies the five-point instances of LM4 B.4 and B.5.

The twenty finite-subgroup classes in type $(0,5)$ The discrete extended mapping class group of a sphere with five unordered punctures has exactly twenty conjugacy classes of finite subgroups, including the trivial group. Seven preserve orientation and thirteen have nontrivial sign. In the following table, the last column lists the fixed-mark counts of all negative involutions, with multiplicity; an empty entry means there are none. \begin{center}\small \begin{tabular}{c|r|c|l} $G$&$|G|$&$G^+$&\text{negative involutions}\\\hline $1$&1&$1$&\\ $C_2$&2&$C_2$&\\ $C_3$&3&$C_3$&\\ $C_4$&4&$C_4$&\\ $C_5$&5&$C_5$&\\ $D_3$&6&$D_3$&\\ $D_5$&10&$D_5$&\\\hline $C_2$&2&$1$&$5$\\ $C_2$&2&$1$&$3$\\ $C_2$&2&$1$&$1$\\ $C_2\times C_2$&4&$C_2$&$5,1$\\ $C_2\times C_2$&4&$C_2$&$3,3$\\ $C_2\times C_2$&4&$C_2$&$1,1$\\ $C_6$&6&$C_3$&$3$\\ $D_3$&6&$C_3$&$3,3,3$\\ $D_4$&8&$C_4$&$1,1,3,3$\\ $C_{10}$&10&$C_5$&$5$\\ $D_5$&10&$C_5$&$1,1,1,1,1$\\ $D_3\times C_2$&12&$D_3$&$3,3,3,3$\\ $D_5\times C_2$&20&$D_5$&$1,1,1,1,1,5$ \end{tabular} \end{center} Thus the type $(0,5)$ total in LM4 B.26 is correct, although it must not be identified with the number of full automorphism groups of individual complex configurations.

LM4 D.28 holds for the full pure three-cusp group Let \(p\) be a prime and \(\rho:C_p\to\mathcal P\) a continuous homomorphism whose multiplier has \(p\)-component one. statement: The literal functor of scan 23 sends a smooth projective anabelian $K$-scheme of dimension at most one to $\Pi_1(X)\longrightarrow\Pi_1(K)$. Its pointed version has morphisms $(f,\gamma):(X',\xi')\to(X,\xi)$, where $f$ is a $K$-morphism and $\gamma$ is an \'etale path from $f(\xi')$ to $\xi$. The path supplies the actual homomorphism of based groups. Passing to paths modulo target geometric conjugacy recovers the unpointed groupoid formulation. For a pair $(X,S)$ the boundary enhancement of scans 28--35 is the following diagram of profinite groupoids, with its displayed commutation isomorphism and its Kummer isomorphism: \[ \Pi_{D^*}\xrightarrow{\rho}\Pi_U\xrightarrow{\varphi}\Pi_e, \qquad \Pi_{D^*}\xrightarrow{\sigma}\Pi_D\xrightarrow{\psi}\Pi_e, \qquad \alpha:\varphi\rho\simeq\psi\sigma, \qquad \ker(\sigma)\simeq\psi^*T . \] Here $D_s=\operatorname{Spec}\widehat{\mathcal O}_{X,s}$, $D_s^*=D_s\setminus\{s\}$, $D=\coprod_{s\in S}D_s$ and $D^*=\coprod_{s\in S}D_s^*$. The map $\sigma$ induces a bijection on components and surjections on automorphism groups, its kernel is abelian, $\psi$ is faithful, and $\rho$ is faithful for hyperbolic curves. The images in $\Pi_e$ are open. After choosing one object in each component, the same data are $p:E\to\Gamma$, its kernel $\pi$, a finite index set $I$, injections $\rho_i:E_i\hookrightarrow E$, open images $\Gamma_i=p(E_i)$, and equivariant isomorphisms $k_i:T\xrightarrow{\sim}L_i=E_i\cap\pi$. The image of $p$ is permitted to be open rather than all of $\Gamma$. Disjoint unions and the separate constant fields recover the non-geometrically-connected version.

statement: For the full CM group the remaining problem is the existence or exclusion of a nontrivial closed procyclic $C\subset R$ whose normalizer in the arithmetic full profinite group has open image in $G_{\mathbf Q(i)}$. Proposition~\ref{A:deeper-common-kernel} below further forces any such $C$ into the strictly smaller group $R_{\rm nil}(F')\subset F''$. No such subgroup has been constructed or excluded here. For a general affine hyperbolic curve the same bare-normalizer problem also remains unresolved here. It is not settled by the primewise theorem or by the cyclotomic-kernel centralizer theorem. The additional restrictions in Propositions~\ref{A:full-support-normalizer} and \ref{A:cm-normalizer-field} below settle cofinite prime support and all normalizer fields containing no CM subfield. Over an imaginary quadratic normalizer field the residual support can contain only split primes. These restrictions apply to the actual full profinite subgroup in this remark. The actual attacks and their exact stopping points are as follows. Lower central quotients and all maximal pro-prime quotients leave precisely $R$. Passing to a finite cover detects every nonidentity element in homology, but its line can have weight one; the proof does not make that character cyclotomic. For a CM detecting factor the restriction to $G_{K^{\rm ab}}$ is trivial, so replacing $K(\mu_\infty)$ by $K^{\rm ab}$ invalidates the no-torus-to-abelian-variety hypothesis: both $T_\ell E_0$ and $\mathbf Z_\ell(1)$ become trivial. The Prym refinement has also been checked directly. For $Y\to U$ finite \'etale, an element in $R$ has proper homology in $\ker(V_\ell J_{\overline Y}\to V_\ell E_0)$. In genus one this kernel is zero, so a weight-one residual detector requires genus at least two. Sending its Jacobian factor to an elliptic curve does not automatically give a punctured map. A map $f:\overline Y\to E'$ restricts to $Y\to E'\setminus\{q\}$ precisely when $\operatorname{Supp}f^{-1}(q)$ lies in the existing boundary. Riemann--Hurwitz then forces $\deg f\leq\deg(Y/U)$. The concrete map $[3]:E_0\to E_0$ on the cover $E_0\setminus E_0[2]\to U$ still surjects onto all of $E_0$, although it detects proper Tate homology. Thus it supplies no such punctured map. Adding punctures requires an arithmetic-equivariant lift; the class-five obstruction above is an explicit case in which that lift fails. A further approach using a normalizer extension as a source for the Hom theorem stops at the same precise issue: it is an infinite-index arithmetic subgroup, not the fundamental group of a finite-type source for which the required open Hom theorem applies. Its projection onto an open Galois group supplies no section by itself. The finite metabelian example above confirms, by an actual mixed-prime element, why primewise tests leave additional information. It is not a counterexample inside $\pi$ to the normalizer assertion. A genuinely new argument on the residual Prym part or a compatible full profinite construction is still required.

statement: Let $V/k$ be a hyperbolic curve over a number field, let $y\in V(k)$, and put $U=V\setminus\{y\}$. For the natural map \[ q_*:\operatorname{Sect}(\Pi_U/G_k)/\Delta_U \longrightarrow\operatorname{Sect}(\Pi_V/G_k)/\Delta_V, \] the fibre over $s_x$, $x\in V(k)\setminus\{y\}$, is the singleton $\{s_x\}$; the fibre over $s_y$ is the entire cusp packet at $y$. For every individual cuspidal class at a boundary point $z$ of $V$, its fibre is one class in the corresponding packet of $U$. Thus $q_*$ induces a bijection from the actual interior point classes of $U$ onto those of $V$ other than $s_y$ and induces an isomorphism on each old cusp packet. For every proper hyperbolic $X/k$ with $X(\mathbb A_k)_\bullet^{\mathrm{f\text{-}cov}}=X(k)$, all its hyperbolic open subcurves have only point and cuspidal sections.

statement: Let $U/k$ be hyperbolic over a number field, $x\in U(k)$, and $\iota:k\hookrightarrow\mathbb C$. Every extension $j:\bar k\hookrightarrow\mathbb C$ gives a dense discrete subgroup \[ \Lambda_j=\operatorname{im}\bigl( \pi_1^{\rm top}(U_\iota(\mathbb C),x_\iota) \longrightarrow\Delta_U\bigr) \] whose profinite completion is $\Delta_U$. Use $x$ for the effective action $\rho_x:G_k\to\operatorname{Aut}(\Delta_U)$, and let $\sigma\cdot j=j\circ\sigma^{-1}$. Then \[ \Lambda_{\sigma\cdot j}=\rho_x(\sigma)(\Lambda_j),\qquad \operatorname{Stab}_{G_k}(\Lambda_j)=G_{v,j}. \] Here $G_{v,j}=1$ at a complex place and is the order-two group of complex conjugation at a real place. The stabilizer of the oriented lattice is $1$. The unoriented orbit is $G_k/G_{v,j}$ and the oriented orbit is a free transitive $G_k$-set of these comparisons. Thus the effective action does not make the discretization independent of the embedding choice.

statement: Let $k$ be finite over $\mathbb Q_p$, let $S/k$ be a hyperbolic curve, and let $X/k$ be a smooth proper geometrically connected curve of genus at least two. Every continuous homomorphism $h:\Pi_S\to\Pi_X$ over $G_k$, modulo conjugation by $\Delta_X$, is induced by a unique $k$-morphism $S\to X$. Consequently the graph construction is a bijection \[ \operatorname{Hom}_k(S,X) \ \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\ \operatorname{Sec}\bigl(\pi_1(X\times_k S)\to\Pi_S\bigr), \tag{B.32.1} \] where section classes on the right are taken modulo the geometric fibre group $\Delta_X$. This closes the intermediate-image case of B.26 for this field and proper-fibre range.

statement: Let $k$ be a number field or a finite extension of $\mathbb Q_p$, and let $S/k$ and $U=X\setminus D$ be hyperbolic curves. Write $\operatorname{Sec}^{\mathrm{nc}}(U/k)$ for the field section classes outside all cusp packets. For each $y\in D(k)$ choose its inertia and decomposition groups $I_y\subset D_y$ and put \[ \mathcal C_y(S)= \operatorname{Hom}_{G_k}(\Pi_S,D_y)/I_y. \] There is a disjoint decomposition, through the actual product and graph maps of (B.32.1), \[ \operatorname{Sec}\bigl(\pi_1(U\times_k S)\to\Pi_S\bigr) \simeq \operatorname{Hom}^{\mathrm{dom}}_k(S,U) \ \amalg\ \operatorname{Sec}^{\mathrm{nc}}(U/k) \ \amalg\ \coprod_{y\in D(k)}\mathcal C_y(S). \tag{B.33.1} \] Each $\mathcal C_y(S)$ is a torsor under $H^1_{\mathrm{cts}}(\Pi_S,\widehat{\mathbb Z}(1))$. The choice of a nonzero tangent at $y$ supplies its origin. If $k$ is a number field, there is the canonical Kummer identification \[ H^1_{\mathrm{cts}}(\Pi_S,\widehat{\mathbb Z}(1)) \simeq \varprojlim_n \mathcal O(S)^\times/ \mathcal O(S)^{\times n}. \tag{B.33.2} \] The right side is a power completion and is not asserted compact. Inflation from $G_k$ is exactly the subgroup arising from the constant units $k^\times$. Thus all intermediate geometric images in a constant family are accounted for by these cusp torsors. The remaining noncuspidal surjectivity question in (B.33.1) is precisely the field-section question already isolated in B.27.

statement: Let $k=\mathbb Q_5$, and let \[ Y=\mathbb P^1_k\setminus\{0,1,\infty,2\},\qquad Z=\mathbb P^1_k\setminus\{0,1,\infty\},\qquad f:Y\hookrightarrow Z. \] A tangential section $s$ at the cusp $2$ of $Y$ is not a point section of $Y$, whereas $f_*s$ is the point section of $2\in Z(k)$. This satisfies every field, prime, subgroup and map hypothesis in the literal interior-point statement of Mochizuki--Tsujimura, Theorem F(ii), and Proposition 3.5(iii) \cite{A_MochizukiTsujimuraRNS}. Thus the stated equivalence for arbitrary dominant morphisms, with point sets $Y(\Omega^H)$ and $Z(\Omega^H)$, is false. The same curves and sections over $\mathbb Q$ refute its unrestricted number-field analogue. This statement concerns that specific reflection assertion; it makes no assertion against the source's RNS Theorem A or its Isom theorems.

statement: Let $k$ be a number field or a finite extension of $\mathbb Q_p$, and let $f:Y\to Z$ be a dominant morphism of hyperbolic curves over $k$. Write $\bar f:\bar Y\to\bar Z$ for its extension to smooth proper completions. For $z\in Z(k)$, the full-section fibre is the disjoint union \[ f_*^{-1}([s_z]) =\{[s_y]:y\in Y(k),\ f(y)=z\} \ \sqcup\! \coprod_{\substack{c\in(\bar Y\setminus Y)(k)\\ \bar f(c)=z}} \operatorname{Packet}_c(Y). \tag{B.35.1} \] In particular, dominant morphisms preserve point geometricity, and they reflect it on noncuspidal source sections. Finite morphisms preserve and reflect point geometricity on all sections. For finite \emph{\'etale} morphisms the latter assertion follows directly from the finite-cover action on the fibre over $z$, without the stipulated local theorem and over every characteristic-zero field.

statement: Fix a hyperbolic type $(g,n)$, its geometric full profinite curve group $\Delta$, and its prescribed peripheral conjugacy classes. Let $Q\subset\operatorname{Out}(\Delta)$ be the closure of the geometric mapping class group, and let $A\subset\operatorname{Aut}(\Delta)$ be its inverse image. For each nonempty stable multicurve type, choose oriented generators $c_1,\ldots,c_r\in\Delta$ of its node groups. Call their $A$-translates, with arbitrary individual conjugations, \emph{pro-simple multicurve tuples}. Let $k$ be a number field, let $E\twoheadrightarrow G_k$ be a profinite extension, and let $\rho:E\to\operatorname{Out}(\Delta)$ be continuous, with the image of the geometric kernel contained in $Q$. The following condition on a continuous section $s$ defines a closed, geometric-conjugacy-invariant subset of its section space: there is a nonempty pro-simple multicurve tuple such that, for every $\gamma\in G_k$, there are a permutation $\sigma$ and signs $\epsilon_i\in\{1,-1\}$ satisfying \[ \rho(s(\gamma))(c_i) \ \sim_\Delta\quad c_{\sigma(i)}^{\epsilon_i\chi(\gamma)} \qquad(1\leq i\leq r). \tag{B.36.1} \] Here the left side is a conjugacy class, so the condition is independent of the representative of the outer automorphism. No outer action satisfying this condition is the peripheral outer action of a smooth marked curve over $k$, or over any finite extension of $k$ after restriction.

statement: Let $k$ be a number field, $2g-2+n>0$, and set $\mathcal M=\mathcal M_{g,n,k}$ and $\overline{\mathcal M}=\overline{\mathcal M}_{g,n,k}$. For a $k$-rational stable boundary object $x$, let $\mathcal V_x$ be the intersection with $\mathcal M$ of the henselian neighbourhood of its residual gerbe in $\overline{\mathcal M}$. Define \[ C_{\mathcal M,\overline{\mathcal M}} =\bigcup_{x\in(\overline{\mathcal M}\setminus\mathcal M)(k)} \operatorname{Im}\bigl( \operatorname{Sec}(\mathcal V_x/k) \longrightarrow\operatorname{Sec}(\mathcal M/k)\bigr), \qquad C^{\mathrm{cl}}_{\mathcal M,\overline{\mathcal M}} =\overline{C_{\mathcal M,\overline{\mathcal M}}}. \tag{B.37.1} \] Isomorphic boundary objects give the same term. For schemes this is the nearby-point definition of Carlson--Corwin; for stacks the residual gerbe and its finite automorphisms are retained as described below. Every section in $C^{\mathrm{cl}}_{\mathcal M,\overline{\mathcal M}}$ has an outer action on the universal geometric punctured curve group which is not realized by a smooth marked curve, even after restriction to any finite extension of $k$. In particular, these sections are non-admissible in the constructive sense of scans 480 and 487--488, and none is the section of an interior moduli point. The same conclusion holds for unordered markings, with the associated finite permutation quotient retained.

statement: Let $k/\mathbb Q_p$ be finite, let $B/k$ be a smooth geometrically connected hyperbolic curve, put $K=k(B)$, and let $f:X\to B$ be a smooth proper family of geometrically connected curves of genus at least two. Write $E_X=\pi_1(X)$, $E_B=\pi_1(B)$, and let $\Delta$ be the geometric generic fibre group. The actual generic-fibre comparison is \[ \pi_1(X_K)\ \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\ E_X\times_{E_B}G_K. \tag{B.38.1} \] Pullback along $G_K\twoheadrightarrow E_B$ induces a bijection \[ \operatorname{Sec}(E_X\to E_B) \ \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\ \operatorname{Sec}(\pi_1(X_K)\to G_K), \tag{B.38.2} \] where both sides are taken modulo conjugation by the same group $\Delta$. Every section on the left is point-theoretic over $k$: for each finite extension $l/k$ and each $b\in B(l)$, its restriction to the point section at $b$ is induced by a unique point of $X_b(l)$. The maps on algebraic sections and on fundamental-group sections fit in the commutative diagram \[ \begin{array}{ccc} \operatorname{Sect}_B(X)&\xrightarrow{\sim}&X_K(K)\\ \downarrow&&\downarrow\\ \operatorname{Sec}(E_X\to E_B)&\xrightarrow{\sim}& \operatorname{Sec}(\pi_1(X_K)\to G_K). \end{array} \tag{B.38.3} \] The upper bijection is extension by properness. This statement does not assert surjectivity of either vertical map for a nonconstant family.

statement: Let $K$ be a sub-$p$-adic field, let $V/K$ be a smooth geometrically connected variety, let $U/K$ be a hyperbolic curve, and let $h:\pi_1(V)\to\pi_1(U)$ be a continuous $G_K$-homomorphism. Write $P_V,P_U$ for the geometric groups. Exactly one of the following holds: \[ h(P_V)\text{ is open in }P_U;\qquad h(P_V)=1;\qquad 1\ne h(P_V)\subset I_c \text{ for a unique lifted cusp }c. \tag{B.39.1} \] In the third case $h(\pi_1(V))\subset D_c$, and the underlying cusp is $K$-rational. In the second case $h$ factors through an actual section $G_K\to\pi_1(U)$; no point realization of that section is asserted. The transfer used here preserves the full geometric homomorphism. More precisely, there exist an extension $K\hookrightarrow F$, a countable field $F_0\subset F$, an embedding $F_0\hookrightarrow l$ into a finite extension of $\mathbb Q_p$, and a descended datum $(V_0,U_0,h_0)/F_0$ whose base change to $F$ is $(V_F,U_F,h_F)$. The base change to $l$ has the same geometric homomorphism through the characteristic-zero base-change isomorphisms, including the peripheral subgroups of the target. These are the actual field maps used; an embedding of $F$ into $l$ is unnecessary.

statement: Let $K$ be finitely generated over $\mathbb Q_p$, and let $U/K$ be a hyperbolic curve which becomes constant after a finite extension: there exist $K'/K$ finite, a finite $p$-adic field $k'\subset K'$, a hyperbolic curve $U_0/k'$, and an isomorphism \[ U_{K'}\simeq U_0\times_{k'}K'. \tag{B.41.1} \] For affine $U$ this hypothesis concerns the whole open curve, including its boundary. Let $\overline U$ be its smooth compactification and $D=\overline U\setminus U$. Then the natural map \[ U(K)\ \sqcup\!\coprod_{c\in D(K)} \operatorname{Sec}(D_c/G_K)/I_c \ \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\ \operatorname{Sec}(\pi_1(U)\to G_K) \tag{B.41.2} \] is bijective. Each packet is the usual torsor under $H^1(K,\widehat{\mathbb Z}(1))= \varprojlim_n K^\times/K^{\times n}$. In particular every proper isotrivial hyperbolic curve over such a field satisfies point-section surjectivity in every transcendence degree.

statement: Let $k$ be a finite extension of $\mathbb Q_p$, choose $q\in k$ with $0<|q|<1$, and let $E_q/k$ be the Tate elliptic curve. Put $B=E_q\setminus\{O\}$. For every integer $n>1$ there is a geometrically connected finite \'etale cyclic cover \[ f_n:C_n\longrightarrow B,\qquad \deg(f_n)=n, \tag{B.42.1} \] whose fibre over every closed point $b\in B$ is the disjoint union of $n$ copies of $\operatorname{Spec}k(b)$. Nevertheless, its generic fibre has no $k(B)$-point, and $f_n$ has no section over any nonempty open of $B$. The covers are compatible under divisibility and determine a continuous surjection \[ \omega:\pi_1(B)\longrightarrow\widehat{\mathbb Z} \tag{B.42.2} \] which is surjective on $\pi_1(B_{\bar k})$ and vanishes on every closed-point decomposition group. Thus the map \[ \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{cont}} (\pi_1(B),\widehat{\mathbb Z}) \longrightarrow \prod_{b\in B^{\mathrm{cl}}} \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{cont}} (G_{k(b)},\widehat{\mathbb Z}) \tag{B.42.3} \] has a nonzero kernel.

statement: For a compact connected oriented surface $X$ of genus $g$, orientation-reversing involutions are classified, up to orientation-preserving homeomorphism, by the quotient surface $Y=X/\langle c\rangle$. The nonorientable quotients have nonorientable genus $q\geq1$ and $r\geq0$ boundary components, with $g=q+r-1$; the orientable quotients have genus $h\geq0$ and $r\geq1$, with $g=2h+r-1$. There are $g+2+\lfloor g/2\rfloor$ types in all. The $g+1$ types counted in the original text of scan 439 are exactly the nonorientable-quotient types. Its margin supplies the remaining types.

statement: Restriction of a number-field section to a real decomposition group is its real component section. statement: Fix an orientation-reversing mapping class $\sigma$ of a compact genus-$g$ surface, $g\geq2$, with $r$ real ovals. The fibre over $\sigma$ of order-two lifts in $\operatorname{Aut}(\Pi_g)$, modulo inner automorphisms, has $r$ elements. The centralizer of $\sigma$ in the orientation-preserving outer mapping class group acts transitively on this fibre. For one lift $u$ its stabilizer fits into \[ \begin{split} 1\longrightarrow\Pi_g^u &\longrightarrow C_{\operatorname{Aut}^{+}(\Pi_g)}(u)\\ &\longrightarrow \operatorname{Stab}_{C_{\operatorname{Out}^{+}(\Pi_g)}(\sigma)} ([u])\longrightarrow1. \end{split} \] The last group has index $r$ in the outer centralizer and $\Pi_g^u\simeq\mathbb Z$. Thus the count $r$ on scans 445--448 is the size of this fibre before the centralizer acts. The unmarked real moduli stack has $g+2+\lfloor g/2\rfloor$ components; with one labelled real marked point it has $g+1+\lfloor g/2\rfloor$.

statement: For $g\geq2$, $n>0$, the components of the real stack with $n$ individually labelled real marked points are classified by an allowed type $(r,a)$ of Proposition~\ref{C-classification}, $r>0$, and the following data. Partition $\{1,\dots,n\}$ into at most $r$ nonempty blocks and put a cyclic order on each. For a nonorientable quotient ($a=1$) identify each cyclic order with its reverse independently; for an orientable quotient ($a=0$) identify the simultaneous reversal of all orders. For a partition of block sizes $m_1,\dots,m_k$ the contributions are \[ \prod_{j=1}^k b(m_j)\quad(a=1),\qquad \frac{\prod_{j=1}^k(m_j-1)!+ {\bf1}_{\max m_j\leq2}}2\quad(a=0), \] where $b(1)=b(2)=1$ and $b(m)=(m-1)!/2$ for $m\geq3$. Sum over the allowed types and partitions.

statement: Let $g\geq2$, and let $\tau$ and $\tau'$ be orientation-reversing involutions of a closed oriented genus-$g$ surface. Conjugacy of their outer actions on the profinite surface group implies conjugacy of their mapping classes by an orientation-preserving mapping class. Consequently the map from the real components of $\mathcal M_g$ to conjugacy classes of involutions in the procongruence extended mapping class group is injective. The same map to the full profinite extended mapping class group is injective. In genus three this distinguishes all six topological types: the nondividing types with $r=0,1,2,3$ ovals and the dividing types with $r=2,4$ ovals. The assertion concerns the images of these six types; it does not classify the remaining profinite involutions.
